verses.130:3: Let Israel hope in the Lord, from now on and forever.
verses.131:1: A song of the steps. Remember, Lord, David and all his gentleness,
verses.131:2: how he swore to the Lord; he made a vow to the God of Jacob:
verses.131:3: "If I enter the tent of my house; if I go up onto the bed of my couch;
verses.131:4: if I give sleep to my eyes, and to my eyelids slumber,
verses.131:5: and rest to my temples, until I find a place for the Lord, a tent for the God of Jacob."
verses.131:6: Look, we heard of it in Ephrathah; we found it in the fields of the forest.
verses.131:7: We will enter His tent; we will worship at the place where His feet stood.
verses.131:8: Rise up, Lord, into Your rest, You and the ark of Your sanctification.
verses.131:9: May Your priests be clothed with righteousness, and may Your holy ones exult.
verses.131:10: Because of David Your servant, do not turn away the face of Your anointed one.
verses.131:11: The Lord swore truth to David, and He will not nullify it: "Of the fruit of your body I will place on your throne.
verses.131:12: If your sons keep My covenant and these testimonies of Mine that I will teach them, their sons also will sit on your throne forever."
verses.131:13: For the Lord has chosen Zion; He has chosen her as a dwelling for Himself.
verses.131:14: "This is My rest forever and ever; here I will dwell, for I have chosen her.
verses.131:15: Blessing, I will bless her widow; I will fill her poor with loaves of bread.
verses.131:16: Her priests I will clothe with salvation, and her holy ones will exult with exultation.
verses.131:17: There I will bring forth a horn for David; I have prepared a lamp for My anointed one.
verses.131:18: His enemies I will clothe with disgrace, but upon him My sanctification will blossom."
verses.132:1: A song of the steps, of David. Look, how good and how delightful it is for brothers to dwell as one!
verses.132:2: Like ointment on the head, which descends onto the beard, the beard of Aaron, which descends onto the border of his garment;
verses.132:3: like the dew of Hermon, which descends onto Mount Zion. For there the Lord commanded blessing, and life forever.
verses.133:1: A song of the steps. Look now, bless the Lord, all servants of the Lord, you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courts of the house of our God.
verses.133:2: During the nights, raise your hands toward the sanctuary, and bless the Lord.
verses.133:3: May the Lord, who made heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.
verses.134:1: Hallelujah. Praise the name of the Lord; servants, praise the Lord,
verses.134:2: you who stand in the house of the Lord, in the courtyards of the house of our God.
verses.134:3: Praise the Lord, because the Lord is good; sing psalms to His name, for it is pleasant.
verses.134:4: For the Lord chose Jacob for Himself, Israel as a possession for Himself.
verses.134:5: For I myself know that the Lord is great, and that our God is above all gods.
verses.134:6: Everything that the Lord willed, He did, in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in all the depths.
verses.134:7: Bringing up clouds from the end of the earth, He made flashes of lightning for the rain, He who brings forth the winds from His treasuries.
verses.134:8: He who struck the firstborn of Egypt, from man even to livestock.
verses.134:9: And He sent signs and wonders in the midst of you, Egypt, against Pharaoh and against all his servants.
verses.134:10: He who struck many nations and killed strong kings:
verses.134:11: Sihon, king of the Amorites, and Og, king of Bashan, and all the kingdoms of Canaan;
verses.134:12: and gave their land as an inheritance, an inheritance to Israel, His people.
verses.134:13: Lord, Your name is forever; Lord, Your memorial is through generation and generation.
verses.134:14: For the Lord will judge His people, and toward His servants He will be moved by prayer.
verses.134:15: The images of the nations are silver and gold, the works of human hands.
verses.134:16: They have a mouth, and they will not speak; they have eyes, and they will not see.
verses.134:17: They have ears, and they will not hear; for indeed there is no breath in their mouth.
verses.134:18: May those who make them become like them, and all who trust in them.
verses.134:19: House of Israel, bless the Lord; house of Aaron, bless the Lord.
verses.134:20: House of Levi, bless the Lord; you who fear the Lord, bless the Lord.
verses.134:21: Blessed is the Lord out of Zion, He who dwells in Jerusalem.
verses.135:1: Hallelujah. Give thanks to the Lord, for He is good, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:2: Give thanks to the God of gods, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:3: Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:4: He who alone does great wonders, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:5: He who made the heavens with understanding, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:6: He who established the earth above the waters, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:7: He who made great lights, for His mercy is forever:
verses.135:8: the sun for dominion over the day, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:9: the moon and the stars for dominion over the night, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:10: He who struck Egypt with their firstborn, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:11: He who led Israel out from their midst, for His mercy is forever,
verses.135:12: with a powerful hand and an uplifted arm, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:13: He who divided the Red Sea into divisions, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:14: and led Israel out through the middle of it, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:15: and shook off Pharaoh and his force in the Red Sea, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:16: He who led His people through the desert, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:17: He who struck great kings, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:18: and killed strong kings, for His mercy is forever:
verses.135:19: Sihon, king of the Amorites, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:20: and Og, king of Bashan, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:21: and gave their land as an inheritance, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:22: an inheritance to Israel, His servant, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:23: Because in our lowliness He was mindful of us, for His mercy is forever;
verses.135:24: and redeemed us from our enemies, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:25: He who gives food to all flesh, for His mercy is forever.
verses.135:26: Give thanks to the God of heaven, for His mercy is forever. Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is forever.
verses.136:1: A psalm of David, of Jeremiah. Beside the rivers of Babylon, there we sat and wept as we remembered Zion.
verses.136:2: Upon the willows in its midst we hung our instruments,
verses.136:3: for there those who led us captive asked us for words of songs, and those who carried us away said, "Sing to us a hymn from the songs of Zion."
verses.136:4: How will we sing the song of the Lord in a foreign land?
verses.136:5: If I forget you, Jerusalem, may my right hand be given to oblivion.
verses.136:6: May my tongue cling to my throat if I do not remember you, if I do not set Jerusalem at the beginning of my joy.
verses.136:7: Be mindful, Lord, of the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, who say, "Empty it out, empty it out, all the way to the foundation in it."
verses.136:8: Wretched daughter of Babylon! Blessed is the one who will repay you your repayment that you repaid to us.
verses.136:9: Blessed is the one who will grasp and dash your little ones against the rock.
verses.137:1: For David himself. I will give thanks to You, Lord, with my whole heart, because You have heard the words of my mouth. In the presence of the angels I will sing psalms to You;
verses.137:2: I will worship toward Your holy temple, and I will give thanks to Your name for Your mercy and Your truth; because You have magnified Your holy name above everything.
verses.137:3: On whatever day I call upon You, hear me; You will multiply strength in my soul.
verses.137:4: Let all the kings of the earth give thanks to You, Lord, because they have heard all the words of Your mouth.
verses.137:5: And let them sing in the ways of the Lord, because the glory of the Lord is great;
verses.137:6: because the Lord is exalted, and He looks upon lowly things, and He knows lofty things from a distance.
verses.137:7: If I walk in the midst of tribulation, You will give me life; and against the wrath of my enemies You have stretched out Your hand, and Your right hand has saved me.
verses.137:8: The Lord will repay on my behalf. Lord, Your mercy is forever; do not despise the works of Your hands.
verses.138:1: To the end, a psalm of David. Lord, You have tested me, and You have known me;
verses.138:2: You have known my sitting down and my rising up.
verses.138:3: You have understood my thoughts from a distance; You have traced out my path and my cord:
verses.138:4: and You have foreseen all my ways, because there is no word on my tongue.
verses.138:5: Look, Lord, You have known all things, the last and the ancient. You have formed me, and You have placed Your hand upon me.
verses.138:6: Your knowledge has become wonderful from me; it has been made strong, and I will not be able to reach it.
verses.138:7: Where will I go from Your Spirit? And where will I flee from Your face?
verses.138:8: If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I descend into hell, You are present.
verses.138:9: If I take my wings at dawn, and dwell in the farthest parts of the sea,
verses.138:10: for indeed Your hand will lead me to that place, and Your right hand will hold me.
verses.138:11: And I said, "Perhaps darkness will trample me, and the night will be my illumination in my delights."
verses.138:12: Because darkness will not be obscured from You, and the night will be illuminated like the day: as its darkness is, so also is its light.
verses.138:13: Because You have possessed my kidneys; You have taken me up from my mother's womb.
verses.138:14: I will give thanks to You, because You have been fearfully magnified; Your works are wonderful, and my soul knows it exceedingly well.
verses.138:15: My bone has not been hidden from You, which You made in secret, and my substance in the lower parts of the earth.
verses.138:16: Your eyes saw my unfinished state, and in Your book all will be written. Days will be formed, and no one will be in them.
verses.138:17: But to me Your friends have been exceedingly honored, God; their rule has been made exceedingly strong.
verses.138:18: I will count them, and they will be multiplied beyond the sand. I have risen up, and I am still with You.
verses.138:19: If You kill sinners, God, men of blood, turn aside from me:
verses.138:20: because you say in thought, "They will take Your cities in vain."
verses.138:21: Did I not hate those who hate You, Lord, and waste away over Your enemies?
verses.138:22: With a complete hatred I hated them, and they have become enemies to me.
verses.138:23: Test me, God, and know my heart; question me, and know my paths.
verses.138:24: And see if a way of iniquity is in me, and lead me in the eternal way.
verses.139:1: To the end. A psalm of David.
verses.139:2: Rescue me, Lord, from the evil man; from the wicked man rescue me.
verses.139:3: Those who have plotted iniquities in their heart were drawing up battles all day long.
verses.139:4: They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent's; the poison of asps is under their lips.
verses.139:5: Guard me, Lord, from the hand of the sinner, and rescue me from wicked men, who have plotted to trip up my steps:
verses.139:6: the proud have hidden a snare for me. And they have stretched out ropes as a snare; beside the way they have set a stumbling block for me.
verses.139:7: I said to the Lord, "You are my God; hear, Lord, the voice of my supplication."
verses.139:8: Lord, Lord, strength of my salvation, You have overshadowed my head on the day of war.
verses.139:9: Do not hand me over, Lord, from my desire to the sinner: they have plotted against me; do not abandon me, so that they may not be exalted.
verses.139:10: The head of their encircling: the labor of their own lips will cover them.
verses.139:11: Coals will fall upon them; into the fire You will cast them down: in miseries they will not endure.
verses.139:12: A talkative man will not be directed on the earth; evils will seize the unjust man in destruction.
verses.139:13: I know that the Lord will execute the judgment of the needy, and the vindication of the poor.
verses.139:14: Yet the righteous will give thanks to Your name, and the upright will dwell with Your countenance.
verses.140:1: A psalm of David. Lord, I have cried out to You; hear me. Give attention to my voice when I cry out to You.
verses.140:2: May my prayer be directed like incense in Your sight; the raising of my hands as an evening sacrifice.
verses.140:3: Place a guard, Lord, over my mouth, and a door of enclosure over my lips.
verses.140:4: Do not turn my heart aside to words of malice, to offer excuses in sins with people who practice iniquity; and I will not have fellowship with their chosen ones.
verses.140:5: A righteous person will correct me in mercy and will rebuke me; but may a sinner's oil not fatten my head. For my prayer also is still in their good pleasures:
verses.140:6: their judges, joined to the rock, have been swallowed up. They will hear my words, because they have prevailed.
verses.140:7: Just as the thickness of the earth has been broken open upon the earth, our bones have been scattered beside hell.
verses.140:8: For toward You, Lord, Lord, are my eyes; I have hoped in You; do not take away my soul.
verses.140:9: Guard me from the snare that they have set for me, and from the stumbling blocks of those who practice iniquity.
verses.140:10: Sinners will fall into his net; I myself am alone until I pass by.
verses.141:1: Understanding of David, when he was in the cave; a prayer.
verses.141:2: With my voice I cried out to the Lord; with my voice I offered supplication to the Lord.
verses.141:3: I pour out my prayer in His sight, and I declare my affliction before Him,
verses.141:4: as my spirit fails from me; and You have known my paths. Along this way on which I was walking, they have hidden a snare for me.
verses.141:5: I was looking closely to the right and watching, and there was no one who recognized me; flight has perished from me, and there is no one who inquires after my soul.
verses.141:6: I cried out to You, Lord; I said, "You are my hope, my portion in the land of the living."
verses.141:7: Give attention to my supplication, for I have been brought exceedingly low. Deliver me from those who pursue me, for they have grown strong over me.
verses.141:8: Lead my soul out of prison to give thanks to Your name; the righteous are waiting for me until You reward me.
verses.142:1: A psalm of David, when his son Absalom was pursuing him. Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my earnest plea in Your truth; hear me in Your righteousness.
verses.142:2: And do not enter into judgment with Your servant, because no one living will be justified in Your sight.
verses.142:3: For the enemy has pursued my soul; he has brought my life low to the ground; he has placed me in dark places, like the dead of old.
verses.142:4: And my spirit has been filled with anguish over me; within me my heart has been troubled.
verses.142:5: I was mindful of the days of old; I meditated on all Your works; I kept meditating on the deeds of Your hands.
verses.142:6: I stretched out my hands to You; my soul is like land without water for You.
verses.142:7: Swiftly hear me, Lord; my spirit has failed. Do not turn Your face away from me, or I will be like those who descend into the pit.
verses.142:8: Make Your mercy heard to me in the morning, for I have hoped in You. Make known to me the way in which I should walk, for to You I have lifted up my soul.
verses.142:9: Rescue me from my enemies, Lord; to You I have fled for refuge.
verses.142:10: Teach me to do Your will, because You are my God. Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land.
verses.142:11: For the sake of Your name, Lord, You will give me life; in Your equity You will lead my soul out of affliction,
verses.142:12: and in Your mercy You will wipe out my enemies, and You will destroy all who afflict my soul, because I am Your servant.
verses.143:1: A psalm of David. Against Goliath. Blessed be the Lord my God, who teaches my hands for battle and my fingers for war.
verses.143:2: My mercy and my refuge; my upholder and my deliverer; my protector, and in Him I have hoped, who subdues my people under me.
verses.143:3: Lord, what is man, that You have become known to him? Or the son of man, that You take account of him?
verses.143:4: Man has become like emptiness; his days pass by like a shadow.
verses.143:5: Lord, bend down Your heavens and come down; touch the mountains, and they will smoke.
verses.143:6: Flash lightning, and You will scatter them; send out Your arrows, and You will throw them into confusion.
verses.143:7: Send out Your hand from on high; rescue me and set me free from many waters, from the hand of the sons of foreigners,
verses.143:8: whose mouth has spoken emptiness, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity.
verses.143:9: God, I will sing a new song to You; on a ten-stringed harp I will sing psalms to You.
verses.143:10: You who give salvation to kings, who redeemed Your servant David from the evil sword,
verses.143:11: rescue me and deliver me from the hand of the sons of foreigners, whose mouth has spoken emptiness, and their right hand is a right hand of iniquity;
verses.143:12: whose sons are like young plantings in their youth; their daughters are gracefully arrayed, adorned all around after the likeness of a temple.
verses.143:13: Their storehouses are full, overflowing from this into that; their sheep are prolific, abounding in their goings out;
verses.143:14: their cattle are fat. There is no collapse of a wall, nor passage through, nor outcry in their streets.
verses.143:15: They have called the people blessed to whom these things belong; blessed is the people whose God is the Lord.
verses.144:1: Praise of David himself. I will exalt You, my God, the King, and I will bless Your name forever, and forever and ever.
verses.144:2: Every single day I will bless You, and I will praise Your name forever, and forever and ever.
verses.144:3: Great is the Lord, and exceedingly praiseworthy, and there is no end to His greatness.
verses.144:4: Generation after generation will praise Your works, and they will proclaim Your power.
verses.144:5: They will speak of the magnificence of the glory of Your holiness, and they will recount Your wonders.
verses.144:6: And they will tell of the might of Your fearsome deeds, and they will recount Your greatness.
verses.144:7: They will pour out the memory of the abundance of Your sweetness, and they will exult in Your righteousness.
verses.144:8: Compassionate and merciful is the Lord: patient, and greatly merciful.
verses.144:9: Sweet is the Lord to all, and His compassions are over all His works.
verses.144:10: May all Your works give thanks to You, Lord, and may Your holy ones bless You.
verses.144:11: They will tell of the glory of Your kingdom, and they will speak of Your power,
verses.144:12: so that they may make known to the sons of men Your power, and the glory of the magnificence of Your kingdom.
verses.144:13: Your kingdom is a kingdom of all ages, and Your dominion is throughout every generation and generation. Faithful is the Lord in all His words, and holy in all His works.
verses.144:14: The Lord lifts up all who are falling, and raises up all who are struck down.
verses.144:15: The eyes of all hope in You, Lord, and You give them their food at the proper time.
verses.144:16: You open Your hand and fill every living creature with blessing.
verses.144:17: Righteous is the Lord in all His ways, and holy in all His works.
verses.144:18: Near is the Lord to all who call on Him, to all who call on Him in truth.
verses.144:19: He will do the will of those who fear Him, and He will heed their supplication, and He will save them.
verses.144:20: The Lord guards all who love Him, and He will destroy all sinners.
verses.144:21: My mouth will speak the praise of the Lord, and may all flesh bless His holy name forever, and forever and ever.
verses.145:2: Praise the Lord, my soul. I will praise the Lord in my life; I will sing psalms to my God as long as I exist. Do not trust in princes,
verses.145:3: in the sons of men, in whom there is no salvation.
verses.145:4: His spirit will go out, and he will return to his earth; on that day all their thoughts will perish.
verses.145:5: Blessed is the one whose helper is the God of Jacob; his hope is in the Lord his God,
verses.145:6: who made heaven and earth, the sea, and everything that is in them;
verses.145:7: who guards truth forever, renders justice for those suffering wrong, gives food to the hungry. The Lord releases those in shackles;
verses.145:8: the Lord gives light to the blind. The Lord raises up those who are struck down; the Lord loves the righteous.
verses.145:9: The Lord guards sojourners; He will uphold the orphan and the widow, and He will destroy the ways of sinners.
verses.145:10: The Lord will reign for all ages; your God, Zion, from generation to generation.
verses.146:1: Hallelujah. Praise the Lord, for a psalm is good; let praise to our God be pleasant and fitting.
verses.146:2: The Lord is building Jerusalem; He will gather the scattered of Israel,
verses.146:3: the One who heals those crushed in heart and bandages their wounds;
verses.146:4: who counts the multitude of the stars and calls out names for all of them.
verses.146:5: Our Lord is great, and His power is great, and there is no number to His wisdom.
verses.146:6: The Lord upholds the meek, but He humbles sinners all the way to the ground.
verses.146:7: Begin singing to the Lord in thanksgiving; sing psalms to our God on the lyre,
verses.146:8: the One who covers the sky with clouds and prepares rain for the earth; who brings forth grass on the mountains and vegetation for the service of mankind;
verses.146:9: who gives to livestock their food, and to the young of ravens calling upon Him.
verses.146:10: He will not take delight in the strength of a horse, nor will He be well pleased with the legs of a man.
verses.146:11: The Lord is well pleased with those who fear Him, and with those who hope in His mercy.
verses.147:1: Hallelujah. Praise the Lord, Jerusalem; praise your God, Zion.
verses.147:2: For He has fortified the bars of your gates; He has blessed your children within you.
verses.147:3: He has made your borders peace and satisfies you with the choicest wheat.
verses.147:4: He sends out His utterance to the earth; swiftly His word runs.
verses.147:5: He gives snow like wool; He scatters mist like ash.
verses.147:6: He casts His ice like morsels; before the face of His cold, who will endure?
verses.147:7: He will send out His word and melt them; His wind will blow, and the waters will flow.
verses.147:8: He proclaims His word to Jacob, His ordinances and judgments to Israel.
verses.147:9: He has not done so for any nation, and He has not revealed His judgments to them. Hallelujah.
verses.148:1: Hallelujah. Praise the Lord from the heavens; praise Him in the heights.
verses.148:2: Praise Him, all His angels; praise Him, all His powers.
verses.148:3: Praise Him, sun and moon; praise Him, all stars and light.
verses.148:4: Praise Him, heavens of heavens; and all the waters that are above the heavens,
verses.148:5: let them praise the name of the Lord. For He Himself spoke, and they came into being; He Himself commanded, and they were created.
verses.148:6: He established them forever, and for age upon age; He set a decree, and it will not pass away.
verses.148:7: Praise the Lord from the earth, dragons and all abysses;
verses.148:8: fire, hail, snow, ice, wind of storms, which carry out His word;
verses.148:9: mountains and all hills; fruit-bearing trees and all cedars;
verses.148:10: wild beasts and all livestock; reptiles and winged birds;
verses.148:11: kings of the earth and all peoples; rulers and all judges of the earth;
verses.148:12: young men and virgins; the elderly with the younger, let them praise the name of the Lord,
verses.148:13: for His name alone has been exalted.
verses.148:14: Thanksgiving to Him is above heaven and earth; and He has exalted the horn of His people. A hymn for all His saints, the children of Israel, a people drawing near to Him. Hallelujah.
verses.149:1: Hallelujah. Sing to the Lord a new song; His praise is in the assembly of the saints.
verses.149:2: Let Israel be glad in Him who made him, and let the sons of Zion exult in their King.
verses.149:3: Let them praise His name with dancing; with tambourine and harp let them sing praise to Him.
verses.149:4: For the Lord finds pleasure in His people, and He will exalt the meek to salvation.
verses.149:5: The saints will exult in glory; they will be glad on their beds.
verses.149:6: The exaltations of God are in their throats, and double-edged swords are in their hands:
verses.149:7: to carry out vengeance on the nations, rebukes on the peoples;
verses.149:8: to bind their kings in fetters, and their nobles in iron manacles;
verses.149:9: so that they may carry out on them the written judgment: this is glory for all His saints. Hallelujah.
verses.150:1: Hallelujah. Praise the Lord in His holy places; praise Him in the expanse of His might.
verses.150:2: Praise Him for His mighty works; praise Him according to the abundance of His greatness.
verses.150:3: Praise Him with the sound of the trumpet; praise Him with harp and lyre.
verses.150:4: Praise Him with tambourine and dancing; praise Him with strings and organ.
verses.150:5: Praise Him with well-sounding cymbals; praise Him with cymbals of jubilation.
verses.150:6: May every spirit praise the Lord! Hallelujah.

notes.1:1: Vulgate "cathedra pestilentiae" ("seat of pestilence") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "seat of scoffers."
notes.1:3: Vulgate "non defluet" ("will not fall away") follows the Septuagint ("will not drop off"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "will not wither."
notes.1:4: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate repeats "non sic" ("Not so ... not so"), renders "pulvis" ("dust") rather than Hebrew "chaff," and includes "a facie terrae" ("from the face of the earth").
notes.1:5: Vulgate "non resurgent" ("will not rise again") follows the Septuagint ("will not rise up"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "will not stand."
notes.2:2: Latin "christum ejus" literally means "His anointed one" (Greek "christos," Hebrew "mashiach"/Messiah), referring to the Davidic king and messianically to Christ.
notes.2:3: Vulgate "jugum ipsorum" ("Their yoke") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "their cords."
notes.2:6: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses the passive voice ("I have been established as king by Him") with the Anointed speaking, and places "proclaiming His decree" at the end of verse 6; the Hebrew Masoretic Text has God speaking ("I have set My king") and begins verse 7 with the decree.
notes.2:9: Vulgate "Reges eos" ("You will rule them") follows the Septuagint ("shepherd/rule," echoed in Revelation 2:27; 12:5; 19:15), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants than the Masoretic Text's "You will break them."
notes.2:12: Vulgate "Apprehendite disciplinam" ("Take hold of discipline") and "de via justa" ("from the righteous way") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Kiss the son" (a debated phrase) and omits "righteous."
notes.3:1: In the Vulgate and Septuagint, the superscription is numbered as verse 1, shifting the remaining verse numbers in Psalm 3 by one relative to Hebrew and most English editions.
notes.3:2: Vulgate "quid multiplicati sunt" ("why have ... multiplied?") follows the Septuagint as a question, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads as an exclamation ("how many are my foes").
notes.3:4: Vulgate "susceptor meus" ("my upholder") follows the Septuagint ("my helper/supporter"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a shield about me."
notes.3:7: Vulgate "millia" reads "thousands," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Septuagint read "ten thousands" (myriads).
notes.3:8: Vulgate "sine causa" ("without cause") follows the Septuagint ("in vain"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "on the cheek."
notes.4:1: Latin In finem, in carminibus ("To the end, in songs") follows the Septuagint superscription, whereas the Hebrew reads "For the choirmaster, with stringed instruments."
notes.4:3: Latin gravi corde ("heavy of heart") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "how long will my glory become shame."
notes.4:5: Latin Irascimini ("Be angry") and compungimini ("feel remorse") follow the Septuagint (cf. Eph 4:26), where the Hebrew reads "Tremble" and "be silent."
notes.4:7: Latin Signatum est ("has been sealed") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads an imperative, "Lift up."
notes.4:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate forms an independent sentence here and includes "oil," whereas the Hebrew compares the psalmist's gladness to the abundance of their grain and new wine.
notes.4:9: Latin in idipsum (literally "in the very same") renders Greek epi to auto ("together / at once"); singulariter in spe ("uniquely in hope") also follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "make me dwell alone in safety."
notes.5:1: Latin pro ea quæ hæreditatem consequitur ("for her who attains the inheritance") follows the Septuagint, which derived the Hebrew term from the root "inherit" rather than "flutes."
notes.5:5: Latin astabo tibi ("I will stand before You") follows the Septuagint (Hebrew: "I will arrange [my prayer] for You"); videbo quoniam may be read either as "I will see that" (following the Latin punctuation) or "I will watch, for."
notes.5:9: Latin viam meam ("my way") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "Your way."
notes.5:12: Latin habitabis in eis ("You will dwell in them") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "You will shelter/protect them."
notes.5:13: Latin coronasti nos ("You have crowned us") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "You surround him."
notes.6:1: Latin Pro octava ("For the eighth") corresponds to the Hebrew musical term sheminit, often understood as an eight-stringed instrument or a lower octave.
notes.6:6: Latin in inferno literally refers to the lower realm or underworld (translating Greek Hades and Hebrew Sheol); confitebitur in ecclesiastical Latin carries the sense of giving praise or thanks.
notes.6:8: Latin a furore ("from fury") and first-person inveteravi ("I have grown old") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "from grief/vexation" and third-person "it [my eye] grows old."
notes.6:10: Latin suscepit ("has accepted") follows the Septuagint aorist, whereas the Hebrew verb is usually rendered as present or future ("accepts / will accept").
notes.7:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate superscription reads "Cushi, son of Jemini" (Chusi, filii Jemini), whereas the Hebrew reads "Cush, a Benjamite."
notes.7:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders this verse as an oath against retaliating against enemies who return evil ("deservedly fall away empty"), whereas the Hebrew reads "if I have repaid evil to one at peace with me—indeed I rescued my adversary without cause."
notes.7:10: Latin "renes" (literally "kidneys") reflects the biblical idiom for the innermost seat of emotions and desires.
notes.7:12: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate adds "strong and patient" and frames the second clause as a rhetorical question ("does He grow angry every single day?"), whereas the Hebrew reads "and a God who feels indignation every day."
notes.7:14: Following the Septuagint dative plural, the Vulgate reads "for those who burn" (ardentibus), whereas the Hebrew refers to "fiery arrows."
notes.8:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew musical heading ("for the choirmaster, upon the Gittith") as "To the end, for the winepresses" (In finem, pro torcularibus).
notes.8:3: Following the Septuagint (and as quoted in Matthew 21:16), the Vulgate reads "You have perfected praise" (perfecisti laudem), whereas the Hebrew reads "You have established strength."
notes.8:4: The Vulgate uses the future indicative "For I will see" (Quoniam videbo), following the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "When I look at."
notes.8:6: Following the Septuagint (as echoed in Hebrews 2:7), the Vulgate reads "than the angels" (ab angelis), whereas the Hebrew reads "than God" (or "heavenly beings").
notes.9:1: Following the Septuagint, Vulgate Psalm 9 combines Hebrew Psalms 9 and 10 into a single psalm (Hebrew Psalm 10 begins at 9:22); the heading "for the hidden things of the son" reflects the Septuagint reading where the Hebrew has "according to Muth-labben."
notes.9:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "swords" (frameae) and "with a sound" (cum sonitu), whereas the Hebrew reads "ruins" and "they themselves."
notes.9:21: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "a lawgiver" (legislatorem), whereas the Hebrew reads "terror" (or "fear").
notes.9:25: The Vulgate describes the sinner refusing to seek God because of his own abundant anger ("according to the multitude of his anger, he will not seek"), whereas the Hebrew depicts the wicked in his pride claiming that God will not call him to account.
notes.9:29: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "with the rich" (cum divitibus), whereas the Hebrew reads "in the villages."
notes.10:1: Vulgate Psalm 10 corresponds to Psalm 11 in Hebrew numbering. "To the end" renders Latin "In finem" (from Septuagint "eis to telos"), corresponding to the Hebrew musical heading often translated "for the choirmaster."
notes.10:3: "what You have perfected" follows the Vulgate ("quae perfecisti") and Septuagint, addressing God directly, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "the foundations."
notes.10:4: "toward the poor" follows the Vulgate ("in pauperem") and Septuagint and is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew. "question" renders Latin "interrogant," denoting judicial questioning or examination (likewise in 10:5).
notes.10:5: Following the Vulgate ("qui autem diligit iniquitatem, odit animam suam") and Septuagint, the lover of iniquity hates his own soul; in the Masoretic Hebrew, the Lord's soul hates the lover of violence.
notes.10:7: Following the Vulgate ("aequitatem vidit vultus ejus") and Septuagint, "His face" is the subject and "equity" is the object; the Masoretic Hebrew is commonly rendered "the upright will see His face."
notes.11:1: Vulgate Psalm 11 corresponds to Psalm 12 in Hebrew numbering. "for the eighth" translates Latin "pro octava" (Septuagint "hyper tes ogdoes"), corresponding to the Hebrew musical term "sheminith."
notes.11:3: "in heart and heart" preserves the literal Vulgate Hebraism ("in corde et corde"), meaning with a double or divided heart.
notes.11:6: "I will place them in salvation; I will act confidently in it" follows the Vulgate ("Ponam in salutari; fiducialiter agam in eo") and Septuagint, where the object of "place" is unexpressed and "in eo" can refer either to salvation ("in it") or to the needy person ("in him").
notes.11:7: "proven to the earth" follows the Vulgate ("probatum terrae") and Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "in a furnace on the earth."
notes.11:9: "according to Your height, You have multiplied the sons of men" follows the Vulgate ("secundum altitudinem tuam multiplicasti filios hominum") and Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads "when vileness is exalted among the sons of men."
notes.12:2: Vulgate Psalm 12 corresponds to Psalm 13 in Hebrew numbering. The second occurrence of "to the end" translates Latin "in finem" (Septuagint "eis telos"), meaning completely or forever, echoing the superscription.
notes.12:3: The Latin text here ends with "throughout the day" ("per diem") and does not include the additional question ("How long will my enemy be exalted over me?") found in the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.12:6: "and I will sing psalms to the name of the Lord Most High" follows the Vulgate ("et psallam nomini Domini altissimi") and Septuagint; this final clause is absent from the Masoretic Hebrew.
notes.13:1: The superscription "To the end" (Latin "In finem," from the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, usually rendered "For the choir director." The Vulgate also includes "there is not even one" ("non est usque ad unum") in verse 1 as well as verse 3.
notes.13:3: The Vulgate preserves the longer Septuagint text of verse 3 ("An open tomb is their throat ... no fear of God is before their eyes"), matching the catena quoted in Romans 3:13-18 and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 14:3.
notes.13:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate includes the closing clause "where there was no fear" ("ubi non erat timor," parallel to Psalm 52:6 / MT 53:5), which does not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text of Psalm 14:5.
notes.13:6: Latin "spes" ("hope," following the Septuagint) corresponds to "refuge" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.14:2: Latin "sine macula" ("without blemish," following the Septuagint) corresponds to "blamelessly" or "with integrity" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.14:4: Latin "Qui jurat proximo suo, et non decipit" ("The one who swears to his neighbor and does not deceive," following the Septuagint) reflects a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants from the Masoretic Text, which reads "who swears to his own hurt and does not change."
notes.15:1: The superscription "An inscription of a title" (Latin "Tituli inscriptio," from Septuagint "stelographia," an inscription on a monument) renders the obscure Hebrew term "Miktam."
notes.15:2: Latin "quoniam bonorum meorum non eges" ("because You have no need of my good things," following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, typically rendered "I have no good apart from You."
notes.15:4: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "Their weaknesses were multiplied; afterward they hurried. I will not assemble their gatherings of blood," whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to the sorrows of those who hasten after another god and refuses to pour out their drink offerings of blood.
notes.15:7: Latin "renes mei" literally means "my kidneys," viewed in biblical idiom as the seat of conscience and inner reflection, and "increpuerunt" means "reproved" or "rebuked" (where the Hebrew Masoretic Text says "instruct").
notes.15:11: In this Clementine Vulgate numbering, verse 11 combines verses 10 and 11, with Latin "in inferno" ("in the underworld," traditionally "in hell") denoting the abode of the dead. Following the Septuagint (and cited in Acts 2:27), the Vulgate reads "corruption" ("corruptionem") rather than the Hebrew Masoretic "pit," and "even to the end" ("usque in finem") rather than "forever."
notes.16:4: The Vulgate "hard ways" (vias duras) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "paths of the violent."
notes.16:11: The Vulgate "Casting me out" (Projicientes me) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "our steps" ("they have now surrounded our steps").
notes.16:12: The Vulgate "They have taken hold of me" (Susceperunt me) renders the Septuagint hypelabon me, differing from the Hebrew "He is like a lion."
notes.16:13: In the Vulgate (following the Septuagint), "Your sword" (frameam tuam) is grammatically accusative as a second object of "rescue," continuing into v. 14 ("from the enemies of Your hand"), whereas the Hebrew treats "sword" and "hand" as instruments ("by Your sword ... by Your hand").
notes.16:14: The Vulgate "from the few of the earth divide them in their life" (a paucis de terra divide eos in vita eorum) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "from men of the world, whose portion is in this life."
notes.17:1: The Vulgate superscription "To the end" (In finem) renders the Septuagint eis to telos, corresponding to the Hebrew "for the choir director."
notes.17:9: The Vulgate reads "in His anger" (in ira ejus) and "from His face" (a facie ejus), following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "from His nostrils" and "from His mouth."
notes.17:27: The Vulgate "chosen" (electo/electus) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "pure"; the verb perverteris literally means "You will be turned crooked," expressing that God opposes the perverse in kind.
notes.17:30: The Vulgate "I will be rescued from temptation" (eripiar a tentatione) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I can run against a troop."
notes.17:36: The Vulgate doublet "and Your discipline has corrected me to the end, and Your discipline itself will teach me" follows the Septuagint tradition, whereas the Hebrew reads simply "and Your gentleness has made me great."
notes.18:1: Latin "In finem" ("To the end," also in 19:1 and 20:1) follows the Septuagint ("eis to telos"), where the Hebrew superscription reads "For the choirmaster."
notes.18:4: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate forms a double negative ("whose voices are not heard") affirming universal audibility, whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered "their voice is not heard."
notes.18:5: Latin "sonus" ("sound") follows the Septuagint ("phthongos," cited in Rom 10:18), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "measuring line."
notes.18:6: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "In the sun He has set His tent" and "gigas" ("giant"), whereas the Hebrew reads "In them [the heavens] he has set a tent for the sun" and "mighty man."
notes.18:10: Latin "sanctus" ("holy") is a distinctly Vulgate reading where the Septuagint and Hebrew read "pure," and "in semetipsa" ("in themselves") corresponds to Hebrew "altogether."
notes.18:14: Latin "ab alienis" ("from strangers," which can also mean "from the offenses of others" in contrast with "meis" in v. 13) follows the Septuagint ("allotrion"), whereas the Hebrew reads "from presumptuous ones/sins."
notes.19:4: Latin "pingue fiat" (literally "become fat") is a sacrificial idiom for an offering being rich and acceptable to God.
notes.19:6: Latin "magnificabimur" ("we will be magnified") follows the Septuagint ("megalynthesometha"), whereas the Hebrew reads "we will raise our banners."
notes.19:8: Following the Hebrew and Septuagint, the first clause omits a verb; Latin "invocabimus" ("we will call out") follows the Septuagint tradition where the Hebrew reads "we will remember/boast."
notes.19:9: Latin "obligati sunt" ("were bound") follows the Septuagint ("synepodisthesan," "were shackled"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "bowed down/collapsed."
notes.20:4: Latin "dulcedinis" ("of sweetness") and "de lapide pretioso" ("of precious stone") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "of good things" and "of fine gold."
notes.20:9: Latin passive "Inveniatur" ("May ... be found") follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew is active; while vv. 9-13 continue the address to the Lord in the Vulgate tradition, some interpreters take the second-person pronouns here as addressing the king.
notes.20:10: Latin "in tempore vultus tui" literally means "in the time of Your face" (meaning Your appearing or presence), and "conturbabit" ("will confound") follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew reads "will swallow up."
notes.20:13: Latin "pones eos dorsum" (literally "You will make them a back") is an idiom for driving enemies into flight; "in reliquiis tuis" ("in Your remnants") follows the Septuagint ("perileimmasin"), whereas the Hebrew reads "with your bowstrings."
notes.21:1: In finem, pro susceptione matutina ("For the end, for the morning support") follows the Septuagint superscription, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "To the choirmaster: according to The Doe of the Dawn."
notes.21:2: The Vulgate includes respice in me ("look upon me"), absent from the Hebrew text, and renders verba delictorum meorum ("the words of my offenses") after the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "the words of my groaning." Similarly in v. 3, non ad insipientiam mihi ("not to foolishness for me") follows the Septuagint against Hebrew "no rest."
notes.21:17: Foderunt ("They have pierced" or "dug through") follows the Septuagint reading rather than the Masoretic Text's "like a lion." In v. 18, dinumeraverunt ("They have counted") is likewise third-person plural rather than the Hebrew first-person singular.
notes.21:22: Unicornium ("unicorns") and humilitatem meam ("my lowliness") preserve the Vulgate and Septuagint readings, whereas the Hebrew text reads "wild oxen" and the verb "you have answered me."
notes.21:32: The Clementine Vulgate reads caeli ("the heavens") as the subject of annuntiabunt ("will proclaim") and quem fecit Dominus ("whom the Lord has made"), whereas the Hebrew has "they shall come and proclaim His righteousness... that He has done it." In v. 31, anima mea illi vivet ("my soul will live for Him") also follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew "he could not keep himself alive."
notes.22:1: The Gallican Psalter reads Dominus regit me ("The Lord rules/guides me") rather than "is my shepherd."
notes.22:2: Latin educavit ("brought up / nourished / led forth") and collocavit ("placed / settled") are perfect-tense verbs throughout vv. 2-3.
notes.22:3: Latin convertit literally means "turned back" or "restored."
notes.22:4: Latin in medio umbræ mortis reads "in the midst of the shadow of death" with no word for "valley," and mala is plural ("evils").
notes.22:5: Latin impinguasti literally means "You have made fat / enriched" with oil; calix meus inebrians ("my intoxicating cup," following LXX methyskon) differs from Hebrew "my cup overflows."
notes.22:6: Latin et ut inhabitem uses a subjunctive purpose/result clause ("and so that I may dwell") following LXX, rather than indicative "and I will dwell."
notes.23:1: Prima sabbati ("On the first day of the week") is a liturgical superscription inherited from the Septuagint and absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.23:4: Accepit in vano animam suam ("received his soul in vain") and proximo suo ("to his neighbor") follow the Vulgate and Septuagint text, whereas the Hebrew reads "lifted up his soul to what is false" and omits "to his neighbor."
notes.23:7: Attollite portas, principes, vestras ("Lift up your gates, princes") preserves the Vulgate and Septuagint reading (repeated in v. 9), whereas the Hebrew text reads "Lift up your heads, O gates." In v. 10, Dominus virtutum literally means "the Lord of powers" or "hosts."
notes.24:7: Ignorantias meas ("my acts of ignorance") follows the Septuagint reading, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my transgressions."
notes.24:8: Dulcis ("Sweet") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of Greek chrestos (Hebrew "good"), and legem dabit ("will give a law," cf. v. 12 legem statuit) follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew means "instructs."
notes.24:14: Firmamentum ("a firm support" or "stronghold") translates the Septuagint krataioma, whereas the Hebrew text reads "secret counsel" or "friendship."
notes.24:21: Innocentes et recti adhaeserunt mihi ("The innocent and the upright have clung to me") translates personal plurals following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has abstract nouns: "May integrity and uprightness preserve me."
notes.25:1: The Clementine Vulgate heading includes In finem ("To the end"), which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (where this is Psalm 26), and non infirmabor ("I will not grow weak") contrasts with the Hebrew "I shall not waver."
notes.25:2: Latin ure renes meos literally means "burn my kidneys," combining the imagery of testing by fire with the biblical idiom of the kidneys as the seat of inward affections and conscience.
notes.25:3: Vulgate complacui ("I have taken delight," following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "I have walked."
notes.25:6: Vulgate inter innocentes ("among the innocent") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "in innocence."
notes.25:10: Latin muneribus literally means "gifts," used here in the judicial sense of bribes.
notes.26:1: The Vulgate superscription adds priusquam liniretur ("before he was anointed," from the Septuagint), absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 27 in Hebrew numbering); illuminatio literally means "illumination" or "enlightenment."
notes.26:6: Vulgate Circuivi, et immolavi ("I went around and offered") follows the Septuagint in taking the first word as a verb, whereas the Hebrew reads "around me" modifying "my enemies"; hostiam vociferationis literally means "a sacrifice of shouting" (joyful acclamation).
notes.26:8: Vulgate Exquisivit te facies mea ("My face has sought You out") follows the Septuagint and differs from the Hebrew, which quotes God's command, "Seek my face."
notes.26:12: Vulgate in animas literally means "into the souls" (an idiom for desire or will), and mentita est iniquitas sibi ("iniquity has lied to itself," following the Septuagint) differs markedly from the Hebrew "they breathe out violence."
notes.26:13: Vulgate Credo videre ("I believe that I will see," following the Septuagint) omits the conditional particle ("unless") found in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.27:1: Vulgate Deus meus ("my God") and the doubled silence idiom ne sileas ... nequando taceas follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "my rock, do not be deaf to me, lest you be silent" (Psalm 28 in Hebrew numbering).
notes.27:5: Latin et in opera manuum ejus retains the preposition in from the Greek idiom for "understand/consider," and destrues ... non aedificabis addresses the Lord in the second person ("You will destroy ... will not build up"), unlike the Hebrew third person.
notes.27:7: Vulgate refloruit caro mea ("my flesh has bloomed again") and ex voluntate mea ("of my own will") follow the Septuagint against the Hebrew ("my heart exults, and with my song"); confitebor with the dative means to praise or give thanks.
notes.27:8: Vulgate plebis suae ("of His people") follows the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew "to them"; salvationum is plural ("salvations"), and christi sui literally means "of His anointed one."
notes.27:9: Vulgate rege literally means "rule" or "govern," whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint use the verb "shepherd."
notes.28:1: The superscription "at the completion of the tabernacle" (Latin in consummatione tabernaculi) and the second command "bring to the Lord the young of rams" (Latin filios arietum, literally "sons of rams") follow the Septuagint and are not present in the Hebrew text.
notes.28:6: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads comminuet eas ("will crush them into pieces"), dilectus ("the beloved," corresponding to Mount Sirion), and unicornium ("unicorns," for Hebrew wild oxen), whereas the Hebrew describes making Lebanon and Sirion skip like a calf and a young wild ox.
notes.28:9: Vulgate praeparantis cervos ("preparing the deer") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered as making deer give birth or twisting oaks.
notes.28:10: Vulgate diluvium inhabitare facit ("causes the flood to dwell") renders the Septuagint's transitive verb, in contrast to the Hebrew "sat enthroned over the flood."
notes.29:4: Latin infernus ("the underworld," traditionally rendered "hell") denotes the abode of the dead. Also, a descendentibus in lacum ("from those going down into the pit") follows the Septuagint and the Hebrew consonantal text rather than "from going down into the pit."
notes.29:6: Vulgate ira in indignatione ejus ("anger is in His indignation") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "His anger is for a moment."
notes.29:8: Vulgate decori meo ("to my beauty") follows the Septuagint, contrasting with the Hebrew "to my mountain."
notes.29:11: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses past-tense statements ("The Lord heard... became my helper") where the Hebrew has imperatives ("Hear... be my helper").
notes.29:13: Vulgate non compungar ("I may not feel compunction," from compungo, to pierce with sorrow or remorse) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "and not be silent."
notes.30:1: In finem ("To the end") is the standard Vulgate and Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical heading ("for the choirmaster"), and pro extasi ("for ecstasy") is a Septuagint/Vulgate addition connected with v. 23.
notes.30:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads second-person Odisti ("You hate"), whereas the Hebrew has first-person "I hate."
notes.30:11: Vulgate in paupertate ("in poverty") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "because of my iniquity."
notes.30:16: Vulgate sortes meae ("my lots") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "my times."
notes.30:23: Vulgate in excessu mentis meae (literally "in the going-out/transport of my mind," rendering Greek ekstasis) conveys sudden dismay or being beside oneself, and ideo ("Therefore") follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew reads "yet" or "nevertheless."
notes.31:1: The Vulgate superscription Ipsi David intellectus reflects the Septuagint ("For David, of understanding"), corresponding to the Hebrew term maskil (a contemplative or instructive psalm); Vulgate Psalm 31 corresponds to Psalm 32 in Hebrew numbering.
notes.31:4: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads conversus sum in aerumna mea, dum configitur spina ("I was turned in my misery while a thorn is driven in"), whereas the Hebrew reads "my vitality was turned into the droughts of summer."
notes.31:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads adversum me injustitiam meam ("my unrighteousness against myself"), where the Hebrew has "my transgressions."
notes.31:9: The Vulgate renders the second sentence with the imperative constringe ... ad te, traditionally read as a prayer to God to curb stubborn people who refuse to come near to Him, whereas the Hebrew describes curbing a horse or mule so it stays near its handler.
notes.32:1: The superscription Psalmus David ("A psalm of David") follows the Septuagint and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text; Vulgate Psalm 32 corresponds to Psalm 33 in Hebrew numbering.
notes.32:6: Latin spiritu means both "breath" and "spirit," and virtus ("power," rendering Greek dynamis) corresponds to Hebrew "host" (the heavenly host); the Vulgate also reads firmati sunt ("were established") where the Hebrew has "were made."
notes.32:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads in utre ("in a waterskin"), reflecting a different vocalization of the Hebrew consonants that the Masoretic Text reads as "as a heap."
notes.32:10: The third clause, et reprobat consilia principum ("and He rejects the plans of princes"), appears in the Vulgate and Septuagint but is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.32:15: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads sigillatim ("one by one"), whereas the Hebrew reads "altogether" (or "all of them").
notes.33:1: The Vulgate reads Achimelech (Ahimelech) and vultum suum ("his face"), whereas the Hebrew reads "Abimelech" and "his behavior/sanity" (cf. 1 Sam 21); Vulgate Psalm 33 corresponds to Psalm 34 in Hebrew numbering.
notes.33:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses the passive laudabitur ("will be praised"), whereas the Hebrew uses a reflexive verb ("will boast").
notes.33:6: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses second-person plural imperatives (Accedite ... illuminamini) and "your faces," whereas the Hebrew uses third-person plural ("They looked to him and were radiant, and their faces shall not be ashamed").
notes.33:11: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads Divites ("The rich"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "The young lions."
notes.33:22: The Vulgate reads Mors peccatorum pessima ("The death of sinners is most evil," intensifying the Septuagint "is evil"), where the Hebrew reads "Evil will slay the wicked"; here and in verse 23, delinquent (literally "will offend/be at fault") carries the judicial sense "will incur guilt."
notes.34:3: Latin effunde frameam literally means "pour out the sword" (a Septuagint-based idiom for unleashing the weapon, where Hebrew has "draw the spear"), and conclude adversus eos takes the next Hebrew term as an imperative verb ("block [the way] against them") rather than a weapon noun.
notes.34:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads interitum laquei sui ("the destruction of their snare") and exprobraverunt ("they reproached"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of hiding a net in a pit and digging a pit.
notes.34:13: The Vulgate reads cum mihi molesti essent ("when they were troublesome to me") and uses the future tense convertetur ("will return"), whereas the Hebrew has "when they were sick."
notes.34:16: In vv. 15-16 the Vulgate preserves distinctive Septuagint readings: flagella ("scourges"), dissipati sunt, nec compuncti ("they were scattered and felt no remorse"), and tentaverunt me ("they tested me"), differing significantly from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.34:20: The Vulgate lacks the negation of the Hebrew ("they do not speak peace"), reading instead mihi quidem pacifice loquebantur ("to me indeed they were speaking peacefully"), and renders "against the quiet ones of the land" as in iracundia terræ loquentes ("speaking in the wrath of the land").
notes.35:1: Latin In finem ("For the end") renders the Septuagint superscription eis to telos, corresponding to the Hebrew liturgical heading usually translated "For the choirmaster."
notes.35:2: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads Dixit injustus ut delinquat in semetipso ("The unrighteous man has said within himself that he will transgress"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "Transgression speaks to the wicked deep in my [or his] heart."
notes.35:3: Latin in conspectu ejus ("in His sight") is traditionally understood in the Vulgate as referring to God (from v. 2), though the pronoun could alternatively refer to the sinner himself as in the Hebrew; ad odium literally means "for hatred."
notes.35:8: The Clementine Vulgate connects v. 8 to v. 7 with quemadmodum ("just as") and follows the Septuagint in reading multiplicasti ("You have multiplied") and tegmine ("shelter/covering"), where the Hebrew begins a new exclamation ("How precious is Your steadfast love") and speaks of the "shadow" of God's wings.
notes.36:3: Vulgate "pasceris in divitiis ejus" ("you will be fed on its riches," following the Septuagint) contrasts with the Hebrew MT, which reads "feed on faithfulness" or "cultivate faithfulness."
notes.36:5: Vulgate "Revela" ("Reveal," following the Septuagint) reflects a reading of the Hebrew root as "uncover/reveal" rather than the MT reading "roll/commit."
notes.36:20: Vulgate "mox ut honorificati fuerint et exaltati" ("as soon as they have been honored and exalted," following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew MT, which compares the enemies of the Lord to "the splendor of the pastures."
notes.36:22: Vulgate "benedicentes ei" and "maledicentes ... ei" use active participles ("those who bless Him ... those who curse Him," following the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew MT has passives ("those blessed/cursed by Him"); in the Latin syntax, "ei" may refer either to the Lord or to the righteous one of v. 21.
notes.36:35: Vulgate "sicut cedros Libani" ("like the cedars of Lebanon," following the Septuagint) contrasts with the Hebrew MT, which reads "like a luxuriant native tree."
notes.37:1: Vulgate adds "de sabbato" ("concerning the Sabbath," following the Septuagint) to the superscription, a phrase absent from the Hebrew MT.
notes.37:4: Latin "a facie" (literally "from the face of," here and in v. 6) is a literal rendering of a biblical idiom meaning "because of" or "on account of."
notes.37:8: Vulgate "illusionibus" ("mockeries," or in late Latin "illusions/delusions," translating Septuagint "empaigmon") differs from the Hebrew MT, which speaks of "burning" or "inflammation" in the loins.
notes.37:12: Vulgate "adversum me appropinquaverunt" ("drew near against me") and "vim faciebant" ("were using violence") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew MT reads "stand aloof from my plague" and "lay snares."
notes.37:18: Vulgate "in flagella" ("for scourges," following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew MT, which reads "ready to stumble" or "ready to fall."
notes.38:1: Vulgate "In finem" ("For the end") renders the Septuagint heading "eis to telos" rather than the Hebrew musical direction often translated "for the choir director." "Idithun" is the Latinized form of Jeduthun, and "ipsi" reflects the Greek dative article.
notes.38:3: "Was humbled" (humiliatus sum) follows the Septuagint ("etapeinothen"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in stillness" (or silence). In 38:4, "exardescet" ("will blaze up") is likewise future tense following the Septuagint.
notes.38:5: "What is lacking to me" (quid desit mihi) follows the Septuagint, contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "how fleeting I am." In 38:6, "mensurabiles" ("measurable") is a distinctive Vulgate rendering where the Hebrew reads "handbreadths," and "substantia" ("substance," repeated in 38:8) translates Greek "hypostasis."
notes.38:9: "You have made me a reproach to the fool" (opprobrium insipienti dedisti me) is an indicative statement in the Vulgate and Septuagint, contrasting with the negative petition in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("Do not make me...").
notes.38:12: "Like a spider" (sicut araneam) follows the Septuagint ("hos arachnen"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "like a moth." The Clementine punctuation also links "in increpationibus" ("in rebukes") with the preceding clause rather than with "corripuisti" ("You have disciplined").
notes.39:5: "The name of the Lord" (nomen Domini) follows the Septuagint ("to onoma kyriou"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads simply "the LORD."
notes.39:7: "You perfected ears for me" (aures autem perfecisti mihi) is a distinctive Gallican Vulgate reading combining "ears" (cf. Hebrew "ears You have dug/opened for me") with "perfecisti" from Greek "katertiso," where most Septuagint manuscripts and Hebrews 10:5 read "a body You have prepared for me."
notes.39:8: "At the head of the book" (In capite libri) translates Greek "en kephalidi bibliou" (the roll or heading of the scroll). The Clementine Vulgate attaches "ut facerem voluntatem tuam" ("that I should do Your will") in 39:9 directly to 39:8 rather than to "volui" ("I have desired it").
notes.39:12: "Have always upheld me" (semper susceperunt me) is a past/perfect indicative statement in the Vulgate and Septuagint, contrasting with the jussive wish in the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("may Your steadfast love and faithfulness continually preserve me").
notes.39:14: "Look" (respice) in 39:14, "immediately" (confestim) in 39:16, and "protector" (protector) in 39:18 follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "hasten," "because of," and "my deliverer" respectively.
notes.40:3: "To the soul" (in animam) follows the Hebrew ("benephesh," meaning desire/will) rather than the standard Septuagint reading "into the hands," while the four verbs here (and "ferat" in 40:4) are jussive subjunctives. In 40:2, "egenum et pauperem" ("the needy and the poor") uses a double expression matching the Septuagint.
notes.40:9: "An unjust word" (Verbum iniquum) and the rhetorical question "Will the one who sleeps rise up no more?" (Numquid qui dormit non adjiciet ut resurgat?) follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "a deadly thing is poured out on him; now that he lies down, he will not rise again."
notes.40:10: "Has magnified treachery against me" translates "magnificavit super me supplantationem," where "supplantatio" literally means "tripping by the heel" or "supplanting" (rendering Greek "pternismon," cf. Hebrew "has lifted up his heel against me").
notes.40:14: "Let it be so, let it be so" translates Latin "Fiat, fiat," which renders the Septuagint's "genoito, genoito" rather than transliterating the Hebrew "Amen, amen."
notes.41:1: Vulgate "To the end. Understanding" (In finem. Intellectus) follows the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew superscription ("For the choir director. A Maskil").
notes.41:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses the future tense and reads "I will pass over into the place of the wonderful tabernacle" (transibo in locum tabernaculi admirabilis) where the Hebrew has "I would go along with the throng." Latin confessio ("thanksgiving") and confiteor ("give thanks") in the Psalms express open acknowledgment and grateful praise.
notes.41:7: In the Clementine Vulgate, "and my God" opens verse 7 rather than closing verse 6. Hermoniim retains the plural form of Hermon (its peaks or region), and "from the small mountain" (a monte modico) renders Hebrew har Mitz'ar ("Mount Mizar") as a descriptive phrase.
notes.41:8: Latin "all Your heights" (omnia excelsa tua) literally translates Greek meteorismoi ("high swells"), corresponding to Hebrew "breakers."
notes.41:9: The Vulgate uses the perfect tense "has commanded" (mandavit), whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint use the future ("will command").
notes.42:1: The superscription "A psalm of David" (Psalmus David) follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew Masoretic Text has no heading for this psalm (MT Psalm 43).
notes.42:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses perfect indicative verbs ("have led ... and brought," deduxerunt, et adduxerunt) rather than the Hebrew jussive ("let them lead ... and bring").
notes.42:4: "Who gladdens my youth" (qui laetificat juventutem meam) follows the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew phrase usually translated "my exceeding joy."
notes.43:9: Latin laudabimur is passive ("we will be praised," rendering Greek epainesometha), whereas the Hebrew uses an active verb ("we have boasted").
notes.43:13: "There was no abundance in their exchanges" (non fuit multitudo in commutationibus eorum) follows a Septuagint reading where the Hebrew means "You did not increase the price in their sale."
notes.43:19: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads the second-person verb "You have turned aside" (declinasti), whereas the Hebrew reads third-person "our steps have not turned aside."
notes.43:20: "In the place of affliction" (in loco afflictionis) follows the Septuagint, contrasting with the Hebrew "in the place of jackals."
notes.43:23: The Clementine Vulgate verse numbering skips 43:22 and combines both sentences under 43:23.
notes.43:27: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "for the sake of Your name" (propter nomen tuum) rather than Hebrew "for the sake of Your steadfast love."
notes.44:1: "To the end, for those who will be changed" reflects the Vulgate and Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew superscription ("for the choir director, according to lilies"), interpreting the Hebrew terms through roots for "end" and "change."
notes.44:9: Latin gutta (literally "drop") denotes stacte, a fragrant myrrh-resin, where the Hebrew has "aloes." Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate links ex quibus delectaverunt te across the verse boundary to "daughters of kings" in 44:10, whereas the Hebrew refers to stringed instruments.
notes.44:12: The Vulgate explicitly identifies the king as Dominus Deus tuus ("the Lord your God") and uses third-person plural adorabunt eum ("they will worship Him"), whereas the Hebrew reads "your lord; bow down to him."
notes.44:14: The Vulgate retains the double genitive ejus filiae regis ("of her, the king's daughter") and reads ab intus ("from within," following the Septuagint, where the Hebrew means "inside the palace").
notes.44:18: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads third-person plural Memores erunt ("They will be mindful"), whereas the Hebrew has first-person singular ("I will cause your name to be remembered").
notes.45:2: Masculine Deus noster literally means "Our God" (rather than "God is our refuge"), and quae invenerunt nos nimis ("that have come upon us greatly," literally "found us exceedingly") follows the Septuagint in making the tribulations the subject, whereas the Hebrew means "a very present help in trouble."
notes.45:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads sanctificavit as a verb ("the Most High has sanctified His tabernacle"), whereas the Hebrew has a noun phrase ("the holy dwelling places of the Most High").
notes.45:8: Latin Dominus virtutum (literally "the Lord of powers," matching the Septuagint) corresponds to Hebrew "LORD of hosts" and is rendered "the Lord of hosts" consistently across the Psalter; susceptor ("upholder" or "protector") corresponds to Hebrew "stronghold."
notes.45:10: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads arma ("weapons") and scuta ("shields"), along with prodigia ("wonders") in 45:9, where the Hebrew has "spear," "chariots," and "desolations."
notes.45:11: Latin Vacate means "cease," "be still," or "be at leisure," and the Vulgate distinctively reads videte ("see") where the Hebrew and Septuagint have "know."
notes.46:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads haereditatem suam ("His inheritance") rather than the Hebrew "our inheritance."
notes.46:8: Latin sapienter ("wisely," following the Septuagint) renders the Hebrew musical term maskil ("a skillful psalm") as an adverb.
notes.46:9: The Clementine Vulgate uses the future tense Regnabit ("God will reign"), whereas the Hebrew has a perfect and the Septuagint an aorist.
notes.46:10: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads cum Deo Abraham ("with the God of Abraham," vs. Hebrew "the people of the God of Abraham"), and distinctively renders the final clause as dii fortes terrae ("the mighty gods of the earth," vs. Hebrew "to God belong the shields of the earth").
notes.47:1: Latin secunda sabbati ("on the second day of the week," lit. "second of the sabbath," i.e., Monday) follows the Septuagint liturgical heading and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.47:3: Latin Fundatur exsultatione ("is founded with the exultation") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "beautiful in elevation, the joy of all the earth."
notes.47:9: Latin Domini virtutum (literally "of the Lord of powers") renders the Septuagint divine title corresponding to Hebrew "LORD of hosts" and is rendered "the Lord of hosts" consistently across the Psalter.
notes.47:13: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads complectimini eam; narrate in turribus ejus ("embrace her; tell it in her towers") and in 47:14 distribuite domos ejus ("distribute her houses"), where the Hebrew has "encircle her, count her towers" and "pass through her citadels."
notes.47:15: Latin reget nos in sæcula ("will rule us through the ages") follows the Septuagint in reading the closing Hebrew phrase as "forever" rather than "even to death."
notes.48:6: Latin iniquitas calcanei mei ("the iniquity of my heel") follows the Septuagint literally, whereas the Hebrew is commonly understood as "the iniquity of my supplanters/foes."
notes.48:8: Latin Frater non redimit, redimet homo ("A brother does not redeem, a man will redeem") literally reflects the Septuagint rendering of an emphatic Hebrew construction ("no man can by any means redeem a brother"), taken either as a rhetorical question or, in Latin patristic tradition, as a reference to Christ; in 48:9, laborabit ("he will labor") similarly reflects the Septuagint reading.
notes.48:13: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads non intellexit ("did not understand") in both 48:13 and 48:21, whereas the Hebrew has "will not remain" in 48:13 and "does not understand" in 48:21.
notes.48:15: Latin infernus (and inferi in 48:16) denotes the underworld or realm of the dead, rendering Greek Hades. The clause auxilium eorum veterascet in inferno a gloria eorum ("their help will grow old in the underworld, away from their glory") follows the Septuagint against Hebrew "their form will waste away in Sheol from their dwelling."
notes.48:19: Latin confitebitur tibi cum benefeceris ei ("he will praise You when You do good to him") follows the Septuagint in shifting Hebrew "men will praise you when you do well for yourself" into a clause traditionally read in Latin exegesis as addressing God.
notes.49:3: Latin manifeste veniet ("will come visibly") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew places the verb "shines forth" at the end of the preceding verse.
notes.49:5: Latin illi ... ejus ... ejus ("to Him ... His ... His") follows the Septuagint in using third-person pronouns rather than the Hebrew first-person ("to Me ... My ... My").
notes.49:10: Latin jumenta in montibus, et boves ("the beasts on the mountains, and the oxen") follows the Septuagint in reading the Hebrew phrase for "on a thousand hills" as "on the mountains, and oxen"; similarly, 49:11 reads "the beauty of the field" for Hebrew "all that moves in the field."
notes.49:18: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads currebas cum eo ("you ran with him") in 49:18 and ponebas scandalum ("you placed a stumbling block") in 49:20, where the Hebrew has "you were pleased with him" and "you cast slander."
notes.49:23: Latin et illic iter quo ostendam illi salutare Dei ("and there is the way by which I will show him the salvation of God") follows the Septuagint in reading the Hebrew consonants as "and there" rather than "and to the one who orders [his way]."
notes.50:1: Latin 'In finem' ('To the end') reflects the Septuagint 'eis to telos', rendering the Hebrew superscription usually translated 'for the choirmaster' or 'for the choir director'.
notes.50:5: Latin 'contra me' literally means 'against me' (or 'facing me'), whereas the Septuagint and Hebrew read 'before me'.
notes.50:6: Latin 'cum judicaris' ('when You are judged') is passive, following the Septuagint (as also quoted in Romans 3:4), whereas the Hebrew is active ('when You judge').
notes.50:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'incerta et occulta sapientiae tuae' ('the uncertain and hidden things of Your wisdom'), whereas the Hebrew speaks of truth in the inward parts and wisdom in the secret heart.
notes.50:14: Latin 'spiritu principali' literally means 'a sovereign/ruling/chief spirit' (reflecting the Septuagint 'pneumati hegemoniko'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'a willing spirit'.
notes.51:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'you who are mighty in iniquity' and places 'all day long' at the start of verse 4, omitting the Hebrew clause 'the steadfast love of God endures all the day'.
notes.51:6: Latin 'verba praecipitationis' literally means 'words of headlong downfall' or 'ruin' (reflecting the Septuagint's 'of plunging down/submersion'), whereas the Hebrew has 'devouring words'.
notes.51:7: Latin 'in finem' ('to the end') here carries the sense 'utterly' or 'forever', using the same phrase found in the psalm superscriptions.
notes.51:9: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'adjutorem' ('helper') and 'in vanitate sua' ('in his vanity'), where the Hebrew has 'his refuge/stronghold' and 'in his destruction/desire'.
notes.52:1: Latin 'pro Maeleth' reflects the Hebrew musical or liturgical term 'Mahalath' via the Septuagint, and 'intelligentiae' ('of understanding') renders the Septuagint translation of Hebrew 'maskil'. In the Vulgate numbering, the superscription is joined with the opening line of the psalm.
notes.52:4: Latin 'inutiles' ('useless', following the Septuagint's 'made unprofitable') corresponds to the Hebrew 'corrupt' or 'tainted'.
notes.52:6: Latin 'eorum qui hominibus placent' ('those who please men') follows the Septuagint ('men-pleasers'), whereas the Hebrew reads 'the one who encamps against you'. Likewise, 'confusi sunt' ('they were put to shame') is passive, whereas the Hebrew is second-person active ('you put them to shame').
notes.52:7: Latin 'converterit ... captivitatem' literally speaks of turning back captivity (following the Septuagint), whereas modern translations of the Hebrew often render the idiom 'restores the fortunes'.
notes.53:1: Psalm 53 in the Vulgate corresponds to Psalm 54 in Hebrew numbering. The superscription "To the end, with songs. Understanding of David" follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "To the choirmaster, with stringed instruments, a maskil of David."
notes.53:5: Latin "fortes" ("strong men") follows the Septuagint ("krataioi"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "ruthless" or "violent men."
notes.53:7: Vulgate "Averte" ("Turn back") is an imperative following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads an indicative ("He will return").
notes.54:3: Psalm 54 in the Vulgate corresponds to Psalm 55 in Hebrew numbering. Latin "in exercitatione mea" ("in my exercise") denotes mental or spiritual exertion, preoccupation, or trial, rendering the Septuagint ("adoleschia") where the Hebrew reads "in my complaint."
notes.54:9: Latin "a pusillanimitate spiritus, et tempestate" ("from faintheartedness of spirit and storm") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "from the rushing wind and tempest."
notes.54:15: Latin "dulces capiebas cibos" ("used to take sweet foods") follows the Septuagint ("edesmata," foods/meals), whereas the Hebrew reads "we took sweet counsel together." Similarly, in verse 12, "usura" ("usury") reflects the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew "oppression."
notes.54:19: Vulgate "ab his qui appropinquant mihi: quoniam inter multos erant mecum" ("from those who draw near to me, for among many they were with me") closely follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew reads "from the battle waged against me, for many are against me."
notes.54:21: In verses 21-22, the Vulgate follows the Septuagint in speaking first of God's hand in repaying, His defiled covenant, and the anger of His face, before shifting via Latin "illius" ("that one's") to the treacherous enemy whose words are softer than oil yet are darts; the Hebrew refers the whole passage to the traitor.
notes.55:1: Psalm 55 in the Vulgate corresponds to Psalm 56 in Hebrew numbering; Latin "a sanctis" can mean either "from the holy things/sanctuary" or "from the holy ones/saints." Latin "Allophyli" (from Greek "allophyloi," literally "foreigners") is the Septuagint and Gallican Vulgate designation here for the Philistines (cf. 1 Sam 21:10-15).
notes.55:4: Latin "Ab altitudine diei" ("From the height of the day") follows the Septuagint in joining Hebrew "marom" ("on high," the end of verse 3 in the Masoretic Text) with "day" at the start of verse 4.
notes.55:5: Latin "sermones meos" ("my words") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "His word."
notes.55:8: Latin "pro nihilo salvos facies illos" ("for nothing You will save them") literally renders the Septuagint (often understood rhetorically as "on no account will You save them"), whereas the Hebrew reads "for iniquity, cast them out" or "will they escape?"
notes.55:9: Latin "vitam meam" ("my life"), "in conspectu tuo" ("in Your sight"), and "in promissione tua" ("in Your promise") follow the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "my wanderings," "in Your bottle," and "in Your book."
notes.56:1: Vulgate 'To the end, do not destroy' (In finem, ne disperdas) and 'for the inscription of a title' (in tituli inscriptionem) literally render the Septuagint equivalents of the Hebrew musical superscriptions.
notes.56:5: Vulgate 'I slept troubled' (Dormivi conturbatus, following the Septuagint) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew 'I lie down among fiery ones'; likewise catulorum leonum specifies 'lion cubs.'
