notes.56:9: Vulgate 'I will arise at dawn' (exsurgam diluculo, following the Septuagint) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew 'I will awaken the dawn.'
notes.57:2: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate casts this verse as a conditional clause with an imperative ('If indeed you truly speak justice, judge what is right'), whereas the Masoretic Hebrew asks a question.
notes.57:5: Vulgate Furor ('fury') follows the Septuagint rendering of a Hebrew term that can mean either 'wrath/heat' or 'venom.'
notes.57:9: Vulgate 'Like wax that melts... fire has fallen upon them' (Sicut cera quæ fluit... supercecidit ignis) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew refers to a dissolving snail and a woman's miscarriage.
notes.57:10: In this difficult verse, the Vulgate follows the Septuagint in reading 'Before your thorns could understand the bramble' (spinæ vestræ rhamnum, vs. Hebrew 'pots' and 'thorns') and concludes with the present tense 'as though alive, so in wrath He swallows them up' (sicut viventes sic in ira absorbet eos).
notes.57:11: Vulgate manus suas ('his hands', following the Septuagint) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew 'his feet.'
notes.58:5: Vulgate 'I ran and went straight' (cucurri, et direxi, first-person singular, following the Septuagint) differs from the Masoretic Hebrew third-person plural ('they run and set themselves').
notes.58:7: Vulgate 'suffer hunger' (famem patientur, repeated in 58:15) follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew means 'howl' or 'snarl.'
notes.58:10: Vulgate 'My strength I will keep for You' (Fortitudinem meam ad te custodiam) and 58:11 'My God, His mercy will go before me' (Deus meus misericordia ejus præveniet me) follow the Septuagint wording and syntax; similarly, 58:18 directly addresses God as 'my mercy' (misericordia mea).
notes.58:12: Latin ostendet mihi super inimicos meos is literally 'will show to me over my enemies' (letting the speaker look upon defeated foes). In nequando obliviscantur populi mei, populi mei is rendered as a genitive singular object ('so that they may never forget my people', matching the Septuagint syntax), though it can also be read as a nominative plural ('so that my peoples may never forget').
notes.58:16: Vulgate passive 'they will be scattered' (dispergentur) and 'they will also murmur' (et murmurabunt) follow the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Hebrew reads 'they wander about' and 'they spend the night.'
notes.59:1: The Vulgate superscription follows the Septuagint in rendering "for those who will be changed" (pro his qui immutabuntur) and "as a title inscription" (in tituli inscriptionem), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 60) has the musical and literary designations Shushan-eduth and Miktam.
notes.59:2: Latin succendit ("set fire to"), Mesopotamiam Syriæ et Sobal ("Mesopotamia of Syria and Sobal"), and Idumæam ("Idumea") follow the Septuagint forms corresponding to Hebrew "strove with Aram-naharaim and Aram-zobah" and "Edom."
notes.59:3: Latin misertus es nobis ("You have had mercy on us") is a past indicative following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew text has an imperative ("restore us").
notes.59:5: Latin compunctionis ("compunction," literally a piercing sorrow or stupor, rendering Greek katanyxis) differs from the Hebrew term for "staggering" or "reeling"; similarly, in 59:6 a facie arcus ("from the face of the bow") reflects a Septuagint reading distinct from Hebrew "because of truth."
notes.59:10: Several Vulgate-distinct readings in verses 8-10 follow the Septuagint: convallem tabernaculorum ("valley of tents," translating Hebrew place-name Succoth), Juda rex meus ("Judah is My king," vs. Hebrew "scepter"), olla spei meæ ("pot of My hope," vs. Hebrew "washbowl"), alienigenæ ("foreigners," vs. Hebrew "Philistia"), and passive subditi sunt ("have been subjected").
notes.60:1: Latin In hymnis ("In hymns") follows the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew superscription (Psalm 61), which refers to stringed instruments.
notes.60:3: Latin exaltasti me. Deduxisti me ("You lifted me up. You led me") uses past indicatives following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew text has a petition ("lead me to the rock that is higher than I").
notes.60:6: Latin orationem meam ("my prayer") renders the Greek word euche ("prayer" or "vow"), whereas the Hebrew text specifically says "my vows"; in 60:7 usque in diem ("all the way to the day") likewise reflects the Septuagint wording.
notes.60:8: Latin misericordiam et veritatem ejus quis requiret? ("who will seek out His mercy and truth?") is a question following the Septuagint reading of Aramaic man ("who?"), whereas the Hebrew text is generally read as an imperative ("appoint mercy and truth to preserve him").
notes.61:2: Latin Nonne Deo subjecta erit anima mea? ("Will my soul not be subject to God?") follows the Septuagint in phrasing this as a question about subjection, whereas the Hebrew text (Psalm 62) states that the soul waits in silence for God alone.
notes.61:4: Latin interficitis ("kill") is an active verb following the Septuagint, and parieti inclinato et maceriæ depulsæ stands in the dative ("as against a leaning wall and a pushed-down stone fence"), whereas the Hebrew text is often read passively ("you shall all be battered, like a leaning wall").
notes.61:5: Latin cucurri in siti ("I ran in thirst") reflects the Septuagint reading edramon en dipsei taken as first-person singular, diverging from the Hebrew text ("they delight in falsehood"); in 61:7 non emigrabo ("I will not depart," literally "move away") also reflects a distinct Septuagint verb rather than Hebrew "be shaken."
notes.61:9: Latin omnis congregatio populi ("all the assembly of the people") follows the Septuagint reading of the Hebrew consonants as "congregation" rather than "at all times," and in 61:8 Deus auxilii mei ("God of my help") corresponds to Hebrew "rock of my strength."
notes.61:10: Latin ut decipiant ipsi de vanitate in idipsum ("so that they themselves may deceive out of vanity together") follows the Septuagint closely (with in idipsum rendering Greek epi to auto, "together"), whereas the Hebrew text speaks of ascending in the balances and being lighter than a breath; in 61:12 duo hæc ("these two things") likewise follows the Septuagint against Hebrew "twice this."
notes.62:1: The Vulgate (following the Septuagint) reads "in the desert of Idumea" (in deserto Idumaeae), whereas the Hebrew text reads "in the wilderness of Judah."
notes.62:2: Latin de luce vigilo (literally "from light I keep watch") follows the Septuagint "I rise early," where the Hebrew has "I earnestly seek"; quam multipliciter ("in how many ways") reflects the Septuagint reading of a Hebrew verb meaning "faints" or "longs."
notes.62:3: The Vulgate attaches "In a desert land, both pathless and waterless" to this verse rather than verse 2, and renders the Septuagint passive (apparui tibi, literally "I appeared to You") where the Hebrew has active "I have looked upon You."
notes.62:7: Latin in matutinis ("in the morning hours") follows the Septuagint ("in the early mornings"), whereas the Hebrew has "in the night watches."
notes.62:10: Latin in vanum ("in vain") follows the Septuagint (eis maten), whereas the Hebrew reads "to ruin" or "to destroy it."
notes.63:1: Latin In finem ("For the end") translates the Septuagint superscription eis to telos, corresponding to the Hebrew term usually rendered "For the choirmaster."
notes.63:3: The Vulgate (following the Septuagint) uses the past indicative Protexisti me ("You have sheltered me") rather than the Hebrew imperative ("Hide me").
notes.63:4: Latin arcum rem amaram ("a bow, a bitter thing") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "their arrows, bitter words."
notes.63:7: Latin defecerunt ("they have failed") and Accedet ("will approach") follow the Septuagint reading of the Hebrew consonants, where translations of the Hebrew generally read "we have perfected a diligent search" and "the inward mind and heart of a man are deep."
notes.63:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "and God will be exalted" (et exaltabitur Deus) and "the arrows of little children have become their wounds," whereas the Hebrew reads "But God shoots his arrow at them; they are wounded suddenly."
notes.64:1: The reference to Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and "the people of the exile" (populo transmigrationis) is a distinctive Vulgate expansion of a Septuagint manuscript tradition absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.64:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses an imperative ("Hear my prayer") where the Hebrew has a vocative participle ("You who hear prayer").
notes.64:8: Latin qui conturbas ("who stir up" or "trouble") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "who stills" the roaring of the seas.
notes.64:12: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "You will bless the crown" (Benedices coronae) and "Your fields" (campi tui), where the Hebrew reads "You crown the year" and "Your wagon tracks."
notes.64:14: Latin arietes ovium ("the rams of the sheep") follows the Septuagint in rendering Hebrew karim as "rams" rather than "meadows" ("the meadows clothe themselves with flocks").
notes.65:1: Latin "In finem" ("For the end") reflects the Septuagint ("eis to telos") rather than Hebrew "for the choirmaster," and "resurrectionis" ("of the resurrection") is a Vulgate/Septuagint addition to the superscription.
notes.65:3: Latin "mentientur tibi" ("will lie to You," reflecting Septuagint "pseusontai") idiomatically conveys feigned or cringing submission before God's power.
notes.65:5: Latin "in consiliis" ("in counsels") follows the Septuagint ("en tais boulais"), whereas the Hebrew text reads "in deeds."
notes.65:9: The Vulgate and Septuagint read singular "animam meam" and "pedes meos" ("my soul," "my feet"), whereas the Hebrew has the plural "our."
notes.66:1: Latin "in hymnis" ("in hymns") follows the Septuagint ("en hymnois") rather than Hebrew "with stringed instruments," and the attribution to David is specific to the Vulgate/Septuagint superscription.
notes.66:2: The repeated clause "et misereatur nostri" ("and have mercy on us") is a Vulgate/Septuagint addition absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.66:3: Latin "ut cognoscamus" ("so that we may know") reflects the active Septuagint construction, whereas the Hebrew uses a passive ("that Your way may be known").
notes.66:4: Latin "confiteantur tibi" (lit. "confess to You") is the standard liturgical Vulgate idiom for publicly praising or giving thanks to God.
notes.67:5: Latin "super occasum" ("above the west," following Septuagint "epi dysmon") differs from the Hebrew, often rendered "through the deserts" or "upon the clouds"; the closing clause "Turbabuntur a facie ejus" ("They will be troubled before the face of Him") is also unique to the Vulgate/Septuagint.
notes.67:7: Latin "unius moris" ("of one manner/mind") renders Greek "monotropous" (Hebrew "the solitary"), and the closing clause "similiter eos qui exasperant, qui habitant in sepulchris" ("likewise those who provoke, who dwell in tombs") follows the Septuagint rather than Hebrew "only the rebellious dwell in a parched land."
notes.67:13: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "dilecti, dilecti" ("of the beloved, of the beloved") and "speciei domus" ("for the beauty of the house"), diverging markedly from the Hebrew ("kings of armies flee, they flee, and she who remains at home divides the spoil").
notes.67:16: Latin "mons pinguis" ("a fat mountain") and "mons coagulatus" ("a curdled mountain") follow the Septuagint rather than Hebrew "mountain of Bashan" and "many-peaked mountain"; in 67:17 "montes coagulatos" is accusative as the direct object of "suspicamini" ("suspect").
notes.67:19: The closing clause "etenim non credentes inhabitare Dominum Deum" is elliptically compressed from the Septuagint and may be construed either as "even those who do not believe, so that the Lord God may dwell" or as "those who do not believe that the Lord God dwells."
notes.67:31: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "in vaccis populorum" ("among the cows of the peoples") and "ut excludant eos qui probati sunt argento" ("so that they may shut out those who have been tested with silver"), differing significantly from the Hebrew text.
notes.68:1: The Vulgate superscription "To the end, for those who will be changed" (In finem, pro iis qui commutabuntur) follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew heading reads "For the choir director, according to Lilies."
notes.68:11: Vulgate operui ("I covered") is a distinctly Vulgate reading, whereas the Septuagint reads "I humbled/bowed down" and the Hebrew reads "I wept."
notes.68:21: Vulgate exspectavit ("expected") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "reproach has broken my heart." In v. 20, Latin reverentiam ("humiliation") renders the Greek noun for shame or disgrace (entrope).
notes.68:24: Vulgate dorsum eorum semper incurva ("bend their back down always") follows the Septuagint (cf. Rom 11:10), whereas the Hebrew reads "make their loins continually shake."
notes.68:27: Vulgate super dolorem vulnerum meorum addiderunt ("they have added to the pain of my wounds") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "they recount the pain of those whom You have wounded."
notes.69:1: The Vulgate superscription adds "that the Lord saved him" (quod salvum fecerit eum Dominus), reflecting a Septuagint addition not present in the Hebrew text.
notes.69:3: Latin revereantur ("be humiliated") renders the Septuagint verb for being put to shame or humiliated (entrepomai), a regular Vulgate Psalter usage also found in 70:24.
notes.69:4: Latin statim erubescentes ("immediately, blushing with shame") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "because of their shame." Latin Euge, euge! (lit. "Well done, well done!") is used sarcastically as a mocking taunt ("Aha, aha!").
notes.70:1: The superscription "A psalm of David, of the sons of Jonadab, and of the first captives" follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew text of this psalm (Hebrew Ps 71) has no heading.
notes.70:5: Vulgate patientia mea ("my patience") follows the Septuagint hypomone ("endurance/patience"), whereas the Hebrew reads "my hope."
notes.70:15: Vulgate Quoniam non cognovi litteraturam ("Since I have not known learning") follows the Septuagint ("writings/learning"), whereas the Hebrew reads "for I do not know their numbers."
notes.70:20: The Vulgate past-tense verbs here and in v. 21 (vivificasti, reduxisti, multiplicasti, consolatus es) follow the Septuagint aorists, whereas the Hebrew uses future forms.
notes.71:6: Latin in vellus ('upon a fleece') follows the Septuagint reading of a Hebrew term often rendered 'mown grass.'
notes.71:9: Latin Aethiopes ('Ethiopians') and terram ('earth') follow the Septuagint where the Hebrew has 'desert-dwellers' and 'dust.'
notes.71:14: Latin ex usuris ('from usury') and nomen eorum ('their name') follow the Septuagint against the Hebrew 'from oppression' and 'their blood'; similarly in v. 12 Latin a potente ('from the mighty') differs from the Hebrew 'who cries out.'
notes.71:15: Latin adorabunt de ipso renders Greek proseuxontai peri autou ('they will pray concerning him'), using adorare in its sense of praying or petitioning.
notes.71:16: Latin firmamentum ('a support' or 'foundation') follows the Septuagint sterigma where the Hebrew has 'abundance of grain.'
notes.72:4: Latin respectus morti eorum ('regard for their death') and firmamentum in plaga eorum ('firmness in their affliction') follow the Septuagint against the Hebrew 'pangs in their death' and 'sound is their body.'
notes.72:10: Latin dies pleni ('full days') follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew reads 'waters of fullness'; similarly in v. 7 Latin iniquitas eorum ('their iniquity') differs from the Hebrew 'their eyes.'
notes.72:18: Latin propter dolos posuisti eis ('because of deceits You have set it for them') follows the Septuagint's elliptical phrasing where the Hebrew has 'in slippery places You set them.'
notes.72:20: Latin in civitate tua ('in Your city') follows the Septuagint reading of a Hebrew form that otherwise means 'on awakening.'
notes.72:28: The closing phrase in portis filiae Sion ('in the gates of the daughter of Zion') follows the Septuagint and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.73:5: Latin sicut in exitu super summum ('as in the exit above the highest point') literally reflects the Septuagint's obscure rendering of this difficult verse; in v. 8, 'make all the feast days cease' likewise follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew 'burned all the meeting places.'
notes.73:9: Latin et nos non cognoscet amplius ('and he will know us no more') follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew 'none among us knows how long'; the unnamed singular subject may refer either to the prophet or to God.
notes.73:15: The Vulgate, following the Septuagint, treats the Hebrew adjective for 'perennial' or 'ever-flowing' as a proper name, Ethan ('the rivers of Ethan'); likewise v. 13 has 'strengthened' for Hebrew 'divided,' v. 14 has 'peoples of the Ethiopians' for 'desert-dwellers,' and v. 17 has 'spring' for 'winter.'
notes.73:19: Latin animas confitentes tibi ('the souls confessing to You') follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads 'the soul of Your turtledove.'
notes.73:20: Latin qui obscurati sunt terrae ('those of the earth who have been darkened') follows the Septuagint's personal rendering of the Hebrew phrase usually translated 'the dark places of the earth.'
notes.74:2: Vulgate "and we will call upon Your name" (following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "for Your name is near."
notes.74:6: Vulgate "wickedness against God" (following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "with an insolent neck."
notes.74:7: Vulgate "nor from the desert mountains" follows the Septuagint in reading the Hebrew plural noun as "mountains" rather than "lifting up," and preserves the elliptical lack of a main verb.
notes.74:9: Latin "vini meri, plenus misto" ("of pure wine, full of mixture") pairs undiluted, strong wine with mixed spices or additives.
notes.75:1: Vulgate "in praises" and "concerning the Assyrians" follow the Septuagint superscription; the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "with stringed instruments" and has no mention of the Assyrians.
notes.75:3: Vulgate "in peace" translates the place-name "Salem" (Hebrew "Shalem") as a common noun, following the Septuagint.
notes.75:5: Vulgate "from the eternal mountains" follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "from the mountains of prey."
notes.75:6: Vulgate "the foolish in heart" and "men of riches" follow the Septuagint, contrasting with the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "stouthearted" and "men of might."
notes.75:11: Vulgate "the thought of man will give thanks to You, and the remnant of thought will keep a feast day to You" follows the Septuagint; the Hebrew Masoretic Text instead speaks of human wrath praising God and God girding Himself with the remainder of wrath.
notes.76:3: Vulgate "with my hands by night before Him, and I was not deceived" follows the Septuagint (with "contra" rendering Greek "enantion," meaning "before/facing"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of the psalmist's hand stretched out at night without growing weary.
notes.76:4: Vulgate "and I was delighted" differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("and I groan"); "I was exercised" (here and in verses 7 and 13) literally renders Latin "exercitor/exerceor" for intense inward reflection or spiritual preoccupation.
notes.76:7: Vulgate "I swept my spirit" literally renders Latin "scopebam" ("swept clean"), a vivid Vulgate image corresponding to the Septuagint's "dug/probed" and the Hebrew's "searched."
notes.76:11: Vulgate "Now I have begun; this is the change of the right hand of the Most High" follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text is commonly read as referring to the psalmist's grief or the years of the right hand of the Most High.
notes.76:19: Vulgate "in the wheel" follows the Septuagint in rendering Hebrew "galgal" literally as "wheel" rather than "whirlwind."
notes.77:12: Latin "in campo Taneos" ("in the plain of Tanis") uses the Greek and Latin name Tanis for the Egyptian city called Zoan in Hebrew.
notes.77:13: Latin "quasi in utre" ("as in a wineskin") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "like a heap."
notes.77:20: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "quoniam" ("Since") and repeats "parare mensam" ("prepare a table") from verse 19, where the Hebrew reads "Look" and "provide meat."
notes.77:21: Latin "distulit" ("delayed") renders Septuagint "anebaleto" ("put off"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "was full of wrath."
notes.77:36: Latin "dilexerunt" ("loved") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "flattered" or "deceived."
notes.77:44: Following the Septuagint, Latin "imbres eorum" ("their rains") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "their streams."
notes.77:45: Latin "cœnomyiam" ("the dog-fly") transliterates the Septuagint singular collective "kynomyian," whereas the Hebrew reads "swarms of flies."
notes.77:46: Latin "ærugini" ("to the blight" or "rust") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to the caterpillar" (or stripping locust).
notes.77:63: Latin "non sunt lamentatæ" ("were not lamented") here and "non plorabantur" ("were not wept for") in verse 64 follow the Septuagint passives, whereas the Hebrew reads "had no wedding songs" and "did not weep."
notes.77:69: Latin "sicut unicornium" ("like that of unicorns") follows the Septuagint ("hos monokeroton"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "like the heights."
notes.78:1: The Vulgate "in pomorum custodiam" ("into a watch-post for fruit") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "into heaps of ruins."
notes.78:5: The Latin "in finem" ("to the end") renders the Septuagint "eis telos" and corresponds to Hebrew "forever."
notes.78:10: The Vulgate "Ne forte dicant" ("May they never say") follows the Septuagint negative construction rather than the Hebrew question ("Why should the nations say?").
notes.78:11: The Latin "posside filios mortificatorum" ("take possession of the sons of those put to death") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "preserve those doomed to die."
notes.79:1: The superscription "In finem, pro iis qui commutabuntur" ("To the end, for those who will be changed") translates the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "To the choirmaster: according to Lilies."
notes.79:5: The Vulgate reads singular "servi tui" ("of Your servant") with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "of Your people."
notes.79:10: The Latin "Dux itineris fuisti ... plantasti radices ejus" ("You were the leader of the journey ... You planted its roots") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "You cleared the ground before it; it took deep root."
notes.79:14: The Vulgate "singularis ferus" ("the solitary wild beast") renders the Septuagint "monios agrios," whereas the Hebrew reads "all that moves in the field."
notes.79:16: The Latin "perfice eam" ("perfect the one") treats the Hebrew noun ("stock/root") as an imperative verb following the Septuagint, and the following "et super filium hominis" ("and upon the son of man") preserves the abrupt ellipsis of the source text.
notes.80:1: The superscription "pro torcularibus" ("for the winepresses") follows the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew musical term "Gittith."
notes.80:4: The Latin "in insigni die" ("on the notable day") translates the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "at the full moon."
notes.80:7: The Vulgate "manus ejus in cophino servierunt" ("his hands served in the basket") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "his hands were freed from the basket."
notes.80:8: The Vulgate "aquam contradictionis" ("the water of contention") translates the place name Meribah (compare Exodus 17:7; Numbers 20:13).
notes.80:15: The Latin "pro nihilo forsitan" ("perhaps for nothing") literally renders the Septuagint "en to medeni an" in the sense of "effortlessly" or "in no time," corresponding to Hebrew "soon."
notes.81:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "in the assembly of the gods" (in synagoga deorum) and takes "the gods" (deos) as the direct object of "passes judgment on" (dijudicat), whereas the Hebrew reads "in the divine assembly; in the midst of the gods He judges."
notes.81:2: Literally "judge iniquity and accept the faces of sinners," a biblical idiom for rendering unjust verdicts and showing partiality; the Vulgate uses the present tense and "sinners" (peccatorum) rather than "the wicked."
notes.81:8: The Vulgate preserves the literal prepositional phrase "among [lit. in] all the nations" (in omnibus gentibus), reflecting the Septuagint rendering of the Hebrew idiom for possessing all the nations.
notes.82:2: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "God, who will be like You?" (quis similis erit tibi), whereas the Hebrew reads "O God, do not remain silent."
notes.82:4: The Vulgate reads "Your holy ones" (sanctos tuos), following the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "Your hidden/treasured ones."
notes.82:8: The Vulgate renders the Septuagint's standard designation for the Philistines literally as "the foreigners" (alienigenae).
notes.82:13: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "the sanctuary of God" (sanctuarium Dei), whereas the Hebrew reads "the pastures" or "habitations of God."
notes.82:14: Latin rotam literally means "a wheel," following the Septuagint rendering of Hebrew galgal, which can also denote whirling dust or tumbleweed.
notes.83:1: Following the Septuagint's interpretation of the Hebrew musical heading ("for the choir director, according to the Gittith"), the Vulgate reads "To the end, for the winepresses" (In finem, pro torcularibus).
notes.83:2: Latin Domine [Deus] virtutum (literally "Lord [God] of powers," vv. 2, 4, 9, 13) renders the Septuagint equivalent of Hebrew "LORD [God] of hosts" and is rendered "Lord [God] of hosts" consistently across the Psalter.
notes.83:6: In vv. 6-7, following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "he has arranged ascents in his heart, in the valley of tears, in the place that he has set," whereas the Hebrew reads "in whose heart are the highways [to Zion]; passing through the valley of Baca, they make it a spring."
notes.83:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "the lawgiver will give a blessing" (legislator, taking Hebrew moreh as "teacher/lawgiver" rather than "early rain") and "the God of gods will be seen in Zion" (videbitur Deus deorum, where the Hebrew reads "each one appears before God in Zion").
notes.83:11: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads plural "thousands" (millia), "to be lowly" (abjectus esse, lit. "cast aside," where the Hebrew reads "stand at the threshold"), and "of sinners" (peccatorum) rather than "of wickedness."
notes.83:12: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "For God loves mercy and truth" (misericordiam et veritatem diligit Deus), whereas the Hebrew reads "For the LORD God is a sun and shield."
notes.84:1: Latin "In finem" ("To the end") follows the Septuagint ("eis to telos") rather than the Hebrew musical direction "For the choirmaster."
notes.84:7: Latin "Deus, tu conversus vivificabis nos" ("God, turning back, You will give us life") is a declarative statement of confidence with the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads as a question ("Will You not revive us again?").
notes.84:9: Latin "in me" ("in me") and "qui convertuntur ad cor" ("who turn back to the heart") are distinctive Vulgate and Septuagint readings; the Hebrew lacks "in me" and reads "let them not turn back to folly."
notes.84:14: The reflexive possessive "suos" grammatically refers to the subject "Justitia" ("its steps"), though the underlying Greek pronoun ("autou") and some interpreters refer it to the Lord ("His steps").
notes.85:2: Latin "sanctus sum" ("I am holy") and "sperantem" ("who hopes") reflect the Septuagint ("hosios," "elpizonta"), whereas the Hebrew has "devout/godly" and "who trusts."
notes.85:5: Latin "suavis et mitis" ("sweet and gentle") follows the Septuagint ("chrestos kai epieikes"), whereas the Hebrew reads "good and ready to forgive."
notes.85:11: Latin "Deduc me" ("Lead me") and "laetetur cor meum" ("let my heart rejoice") follow the Septuagint ("hodegeson me," "euphrantheto"), whereas the Hebrew reads "Teach me" and "unite my heart."
notes.85:13: Latin "ex inferno inferiori" literally means "from the lower hell" (or "lower underworld"), reflecting the Septuagint ("hadou katotatou") and corresponding to the Hebrew "depths of Sheol."
notes.85:16: Latin "imperium" ("dominion," also "authority") renders the Septuagint "kratos" ("might/rule"), where the Hebrew has "strength"; "puero" (literally "boy/child") renders Greek "paidi" in the sense of "servant."
notes.86:1: Latin "Fundamenta ejus" uses the plural "foundations," and "ejus" is gender-neutral ("Her/Its" referring to Zion, or "His" referring to the Lord).
notes.86:4: Latin "alienigenae" ("foreigners"), "populus Aethiopum" ("the people of the Ethiopians"), and "hi fuerunt illic" ("these were there") follow the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "Philistia," "Cush," and "this one was born there."
notes.86:5: Latin "Numquid Sion dicet" ("Will Zion say") is a distinctive Vulgate reading arising from a Greek variant ("meti" for "meter," "mother"), whereas the Hebrew reads "And of Zion it shall be said"; "Homo et homo" ("Man and man") is a literal distributive idiom meaning "one person after another."
notes.86:6: Latin "et principum" ("and of princes") and "fuerunt" ("were") follow the Septuagint; the Hebrew lacks "and of princes" and reads "was born."
notes.86:7: Latin "Sicut laetantium omnium habitatio est in te" follows the Septuagint ("as of all who rejoice, the dwelling is in you"), differing notably from the Hebrew ("Singers and dancers alike say, 'All my springs are in you'").
notes.87:1: Latin 'in finem' ('to the end') and 'Intellectus' ('Understanding') are distinctive Vulgate superscriptions following the Septuagint for the Hebrew headings ('for the choir director' and 'Maskil').
notes.87:6: Vulgate 'liber' ('free') and 'vulnerati' ('the wounded') follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew text is commonly rendered 'forsaken' and 'the slain'.
notes.87:11: Vulgate 'medici' ('physicians') follows the Septuagint in reading the Hebrew consonants for 'shades of the dead' as 'healers'.
notes.87:15: Vulgate reads 'orationem meam' ('my prayer'), a distinctive reading where the Hebrew and Septuagint read 'my soul'.
notes.87:19: Vulgate 'a miseria' ('because of misery') follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew text reads 'darkness'.
notes.88:3: Vulgate reads second-person 'dixisti' ('You have said', following the Septuagint) rather than the Hebrew first-person 'I said', while retaining 'veritas tua' ('Your truth') in the following clause.
notes.88:11: Vulgate 'superbum' ('the proud one') and 'vulneratum' ('a wounded man') follow the Septuagint where the Hebrew text reads 'Rahab' and 'one who is slain'; similarly, 88:13 has 'mare' ('the sea') where Hebrew has 'south'.
notes.88:36: The Latin literally uses the biblical oath formula 'si David mentiar' ('if I should lie to David'), an idiomatic emphatic denial meaning 'I will not lie to David'.
notes.88:45: Vulgate 'Destruxisti eum ab emundatione' ('You have destroyed him from purification') follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew text is commonly rendered 'You have made his splendor cease'.
notes.88:52: Vulgate 'commutationem' ('exchange', following the Septuagint) stands where the Hebrew text reads 'footsteps'; in 88:53 Latin 'Fiat, fiat' ('So be it, so be it') translates Hebrew 'Amen, amen'.
notes.89:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "things that are counted as nothing will be their years," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "You sweep them away as with a flood; they are like a dream."
notes.89:8: Latin "sæculum nostrum" ("our age" or "our lifetime") follows the Septuagint reading of the Hebrew consonants, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "our secret sins."
notes.89:9: Latin "sicut aranea meditabuntur" ("will meditate like a spider") follows the Septuagint's rendering of the Hebrew root for "murmur/meditate" (MT: "we finish our years like a sigh"), evoking the fragile labor of a spider.
notes.89:10: Latin "supervenit mansuetudo, et corripiemur" ("gentleness has arrived, and we will be corrected") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "it soon passes, and we fly away."
notes.89:12: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate attaches "dinumerare" ("to count") to the question of v. 11 and reads "Dexteram tuam" ("Your right hand"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "teach us to number our days."
notes.90:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "in the help of the Most High" and "in the protection of the God of heaven," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "in the shelter of the Most High" and "in the shadow of the Almighty."
notes.90:3: Latin "liberavit me ... a verbo aspero" ("He has delivered me ... from a harsh word") follows the Septuagint tradition reading Hebrew "davar" ("word"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "He will deliver you ... from deadly pestilence" ("dever").
notes.90:6: Latin "negotio" ("matter" or "business") and "incursu, et dæmonio meridiano" ("assault and the noonday demon") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "pestilence" and "destruction that wastes at noonday."
notes.90:13: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate names "the asp and the basilisk," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "the lion and the cobra."
notes.91:11: Latin "unicornis" ("unicorn") and "senectus mea in misericordia uberi" ("my old age in rich mercy") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Text reads "wild ox" and "I have been anointed with fresh oil."
notes.91:13: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "will be multiplied" (matching v. 15) and in v. 14 adds "of the house" before "of our God," whereas the Masoretic Text reads "will grow tall."
notes.91:15: Latin "bene patientes erunt" ("will be well-enduring") is a literal rendering of the Septuagint "eupathountes" ("faring well" or "thriving"), whereas the Masoretic Text reads "full of sap and green."
notes.92:1: The Vulgate superscription (absent in the Hebrew Masoretic Text) follows the Septuagint in assigning this psalm to the day before the Sabbath (Friday), while rendering the Greek 'was inhabited' as 'was founded' (fundata est).
notes.92:2: Latin 'ex tunc' ('from then') literally mirrors the Septuagint, linking the preparation of God's throne to the primordial founding of the earth.
notes.92:4: The Clementine Vulgate attaches 'a vocibus aquarum multarum' ('from the voices of many waters') to the end of verse 3, whereas the Hebrew reads it as a comparative ('more than the roar of many waters') introducing verse 4.
notes.93:1: The superscription 'quarta sabbati' (lit. 'fourth of the Sabbath,' i.e., Wednesday, the fourth day of the week) comes from the Septuagint and is absent in the Hebrew; 'libere egit' ('has acted freely') follows the Septuagint past indicative rather than the Hebrew imperative ('shine forth').
notes.93:15: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate connects this verse to verse 14 with 'quoadusque' ('until'), whereas the Hebrew starts a new clause ('for judgment will return to righteousness').
notes.93:17: Latin 'in inferno' ('in the underworld,' traditionally 'hell') translates the Septuagint's 'Hades,' whereas the Hebrew reads 'silence.'
notes.93:20: The Vulgate's second-person verb 'qui fingis' ('who fashion') attaches grammatically to 'tibi' ('You,' God, understood by Augustine as God appointing toil in His commandment), whereas the Hebrew uses a third-person participle describing the wicked throne framing mischief by statute.
notes.93:22: Latin 'in adjutorium spei meae' ('a help of my hope') follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads 'the rock of my refuge.'
notes.94:1: The superscription derives from the Septuagint (absent in the Hebrew), and 'Deo salutari nostro' ('God our Savior') follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew has 'the rock of our salvation.'
notes.94:4: Latin 'omnes fines terrae' ('all the ends of the earth') follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads 'the depths of the earth.'
notes.94:6: Latin 'ploremus' ('let us weep') follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads 'let us kneel.'
notes.94:9: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders the Hebrew place names Meribah ('Provocation') and Massah ('Testing') as common nouns ('in irritatione' and 'diem tentationis').
notes.94:11: Latin 'Si introibunt in requiem meam' (lit. 'If they will enter into My rest') preserves the biblical Hebraic oath idiom expressing emphatic negation ('They will not enter into My rest').
notes.95:1: The Vulgate and Septuagint include this superscription referring to the post-exilic rebuilding of the Temple ("the house"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 96) has no superscription.
notes.95:5: Following the Septuagint ("daimonia"), the Vulgate reads "dæmonia" ("demons"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "idols" or "worthless things."
notes.95:6: The Vulgate follows the Septuagint in reading "confessio et pulchritudo" ("thanksgiving/praise and beauty") and "sanctimonia et magnificentia in sanctificatione ejus" ("holiness and magnificence in His sanctuary"), where the Hebrew has "splendor and majesty" and "strength and beauty in His sanctuary."
notes.95:9: Following the Septuagint ("en aule hagia autou"), the Vulgate reads "in atrio sancto ejus" ("in His holy court"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in holy splendor" (or "holy attire").
notes.95:10: Latin "correxit" (literally "set straight" or "set right," rendering Greek "katōrthōsen") corresponds to "is established" in Hebrew; similarly in v. 11, "commoveatur" ("be shaken") reflects the Septuagint verb rather than the Hebrew "roar."
notes.96:1: This superscription is unique to the Vulgate and Septuagint (Psalm 97 in Hebrew has none); Latin "Huic David" ("For this David") reflects the Greek dative article with a demonstrative, and "restituta est" refers to the restoration of his land.
notes.96:2: Latin "correctio" (literally "setting straight" or "right ordering," rendering Greek "katorthōsis") corresponds to "foundation" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.96:5: The Clementine Vulgate reads nominative "omnis terra" ("all the earth," continuing the ellipsis from the preceding clause), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text and Greek Septuagint read the genitive ("the Lord of all the earth").
notes.96:7: Following the Septuagint (also quoted in Hebrews 1:6), the Vulgate reads "omnes angeli ejus" ("all His angels"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "all gods."
notes.96:11: Following the Septuagint ("aneteilen"), the Vulgate reads "orta est" ("has risen") with singular "justo" ("for the righteous one"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "is sown"; similarly in v. 10, the Vulgate has singular "peccatoris" ("of the sinner") rather than plural "of the wicked."
notes.97:1: The Vulgate and Septuagint attribute this psalm to David ("Psalmus ipsi David"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Psalm 98) reads simply "A psalm." Latin "salvavit sibi" literally means "has saved for Himself," expressing salvation achieved without a stated direct object.
notes.97:6: Following the Septuagint ("elatais"), the Vulgate adds the adjective "ductilibus" ("hammered" or "beaten" metal) to "tubis" ("trumpets"), and distinguishes the shofar as "tubæ corneæ" ("a horn trumpet").
notes.97:7: Following the Septuagint ("saleuthētō"), the Vulgate reads "moveatur" ("be moved"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "let the sea roar."
notes.97:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses future indicative verbs ("plaudent," "exsultabunt": "will clap," "will exult") rather than the jussive ("let ... clap/sing") of the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.98:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate includes the superscription 'A psalm of David himself' (literally 'to/for David himself'), which is absent from the Hebrew, and reads irascantur ('let them be angry') rather than Hebrew 'let them tremble'.
notes.98:3: Latin terribile et sanctum est uses neuter singular adjectives agreeing with nomen ('name'), giving 'for it is fearsome and holy', whereas the Hebrew reads 'Your great and awesome name; holy is He'.
notes.98:4: Latin honor regis ('the honor of the king') reflects the Septuagint rather than Hebrew 'strength of the king'; directiones (plural, literally 'straightenings' or 'directions') translates Greek euthytetas ('uprightness, equity').
notes.98:5: Latin adorate scabellum takes a direct object ('worship the footstool', without Hebrew's 'at') and follows with neuter quoniam sanctum est ('for it is holy'), referring to the footstool rather than Hebrew 'for He is holy'.
notes.98:8: Latin adinventiones literally means 'inventions' or 'contrivances' (rendering Greek epitedeumata, 'practices, doings'), and includes omnes ('all'), which is absent from the Hebrew.
notes.99:1: Latin in confessione literally means 'in confession', used throughout the Vulgate Psalter for public thanksgiving and praise; the Vulgate numbers this superscription as verse 1, shifting the remaining verses by one compared to the Hebrew.
notes.99:2: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads Deo ('to God') rather than the Hebrew divine name ('to the Lord') and in exsultatione ('with exultation') rather than Hebrew 'with joyful singing'.
notes.99:3: Latin et non ipsi nos ('and not we ourselves') follows the Septuagint and the Hebrew written text (Ketiv), whereas many Hebrew-based translations follow the marginal reading (Qere), 'and we are His'.
notes.99:5: Latin suavis ('sweet', also 'kind' or 'pleasant') renders Greek chrestos where the Hebrew has 'good'; likewise veritas ('truth') follows Greek aletheia against Hebrew 'faithfulness'.
notes.100:2: From verse 2b through verse 6 and in verse 8, the Vulgate follows the Septuagint in using past tenses (imperfect and perfect) to recount David's habitual conduct, whereas the Hebrew uses imperfect verbs usually translated as future resolutions.
notes.100:4: The Vulgate splits the clause across verses 3-4, making cor pravum ('a perverse heart') the subject of non adhaesit mihi ('did not cling to me') and joining declinantem a me ('turning away from me') to malignum ('the wicked one'), reflecting the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew clause division.
notes.100:5: Latin persequebar ('I pursued') and cum hoc non edebam ('with him I did not eat') follow the Septuagint against the Hebrew ('I will destroy' and 'I will not endure', the latter from reading the Hebrew verb as 'eat' rather than 'be able/endure').
notes.100:7: Latin superbiam ('pride') and iniqua ('iniquitous things') follow the Septuagint against Hebrew 'deceit' and 'lies'; intransitive non direxit (literally 'did not go straight') means 'did not succeed' or 'prosper' (past tense, against Hebrew future 'will not be established').
notes.100:8: Latin In matutino ('In the morning', singular) and peccatores ('sinners') follow the Septuagint against Hebrew 'every morning' and 'wicked'.
notes.101:4: Latin cremium means dry firewood or kindling (following the Septuagint phrygion), whereas the Hebrew reads "like a hearth."
notes.101:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate names a "pelican" (pellicano) and a "night-raven" (nycticorax, a nocturnal owl), and reads in domicilio ("in a dwelling") where the Hebrew has "among the ruins."
notes.101:9: The Vulgate (following the Septuagint) reads qui laudabant me ("those who praised me"), whereas the Hebrew reads "those who rage against me" (or "deride me"), reflecting two senses of the Hebrew root halal.
notes.101:21: Literally "the children of those put to death" (filios interemptorum, following the Septuagint's perfect passive participle), where the Hebrew idiom means "those doomed to die."
notes.101:24: A notable Vulgate reading following the Septuagint ("He answered Him in the way of his strength: 'Tell me the fewness of my days'"), whereas the Hebrew reads "He has broken my strength in the way; He has shortened my days." In 101:29 the Vulgate also reads in saeculum dirigetur ("will be directed forever"), where the Hebrew has "will be established before You."
notes.102:5: Latin desiderium tuum ("your desire") follows the Septuagint (epithymian), where the Hebrew has a rare noun often rendered "your years" or "your prime."
notes.102:6: Latin misericordias ("acts of mercy") follows the Septuagint (eleemosynas), whereas the Hebrew reads "righteous deeds."
notes.102:7: Latin voluntates suas is literally plural ("His wills," following the Septuagint thelemata), whereas the Hebrew reads "His deeds."
notes.102:9: Latin comminabitur literally means "will threaten," whereas the Hebrew means "will keep His anger."
notes.102:16: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate makes locum suum ("his place") the direct object ("he will no longer know his place"), whereas the Hebrew makes "its place" the subject ("its place knows it no more").
notes.103:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate includes the superscription 'To David himself' (absent in the Masoretic Text, where this is Psalm 104). Latin confessionem (literally 'confession') here carries its ecclesiastical sense of praise and acknowledgment, where the Hebrew reads 'majesty.'
notes.103:11: Vulgate expectabunt ('will wait') follows the Septuagint, whereas the Masoretic Text reads 'quench' their thirst. In the Latin grammar, omnes bestiae is nominative plural, making the beasts the subject of potabunt ('will drink').
notes.103:15: The unexpressed third-person singular subject of ut exhilaret ('so that he may cheer') is ambiguous in Latin and may be understood either as man (from preceding hominis) or as God.
notes.103:17: Vulgate herodii domus dux est eorum ('the house of the heron is their leader') follows the Septuagint, where the Masoretic Text reads that the stork has its home in the fir trees.
notes.103:25: Latin spatiosum manibus (literally 'spacious of hands') preserves a literal biblical idiom expressing vast breadth in every direction.
notes.104:4: Latin et confirmamini ("and be strengthened"), following the Septuagint, differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "and His strength."
notes.104:18: Latin ferrum pertransiit animam ejus makes "iron" the grammatical subject ("iron passed through his soul"), a distinctive Vulgate reading compared with the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("his neck was put in iron").
notes.104:19: Latin inflammavit ("inflamed") renders Greek epyrosen ("tried or refined by fire," corresponding to Hebrew "tested"), carrying the metaphor of purifying metal in fire as well as kindling ardor.
notes.104:22: Latin ut erudiret principes ejus sicut semetipsum ("so that he might instruct his princes like himself") follows the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("to bind his princes at his pleasure").
notes.104:28: Latin et non exacerbavit sermones suos ("and He did not embitter His words") uses a singular verb with a reflexive pronoun referring to God, a distinctive Vulgate reading differing from both the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("and they did not rebel against His words") and most Septuagint witnesses ("and they provoked His words").
notes.105:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate has plural "us" in v. 4 and the second-person passive "ut lauderis" ("so that You may be praised") here, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text (Ps 106:4-5) uses first-person singular ("Remember me... that I may glory").
notes.105:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "ascendentes in mare" ("as they went up into the sea"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "by the sea."
notes.105:15: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "saturitatem" ("satiety" or "fullness," implying surfeit as in Num 11:20), where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "leanness" or "a wasting disease."
notes.105:33: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "distinxit in labiis suis" ("made a distinction with his lips"), traditionally taken to mean speaking hesitantly or waveringly, where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "spoke rashly."
notes.105:48: The Vulgate uses the future indicative "dicet" ("will say") and translates the closing Hebrew acclamation ("Amen, Amen") as Latin "Fiat, fiat" ("So be it, so be it").
notes.106:8: In the Vulgate (and vv. 15, 21, 31), 'His mercies' (misericordiae ejus) is nominative plural and serves as the grammatical subject of 'give thanks' (confiteantur), reflecting the ambiguous neuter plural of the Septuagint; the Hebrew instead makes the redeemed the subject giving thanks to the Lord for His mercies.
notes.106:10: The Vulgate uses accusative participles (sedentes ... vinctos) with no finite verb and reads 'in destitution' (in mendicitate, following the Septuagint's 'poverty'), whereas the Hebrew has 'in affliction.'
notes.106:17: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads 'He took them up' (Suscepit eos), whereas the Hebrew text begins the verse with 'Fools.'
notes.106:37: The Vulgate's 'fruit of birth' (fructum nativitatis) reflects the Septuagint Greek noun for 'yield' or 'produce' (genematos), rendered in Latin according to its cognate sense of 'birth' or 'offspring.'
notes.107:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate includes 'Arise, my glory' in this verse and reads 'I will arise at dawn' (exsurgam diluculo), whereas the Hebrew reads 'I will awaken the dawn.'
notes.107:7: Following the Clementine Vulgate punctuation, the clause 'so that Your beloved ones may be freed' completes the petition of v. 6 rather than introducing 'Save by Your right hand.'
notes.107:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Succoth literally as a common noun, 'the valley of tents' (convallem tabernaculorum).
notes.107:9: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders Ephraim as 'the support of My head' (susceptio capitis mei) and Judah as 'My king' (rex meus), where the Hebrew reads 'helmet' and 'scepter' (or 'lawgiver').
notes.107:10: Distinctively Vulgate readings here include 'the basin of My hope' (lebes spei meae, vs. Hebrew 'washbasin') and 'to Me foreigners have been made friends' (mihi alienigenae amici facti sunt, vs. Hebrew 'over Philistia I shout in triumph'); 'Edom' renders the Greco-Latin name Idumaeam (also in v. 11).
notes.108:2: Vulgate 'laudem meam ne tacueris' takes 'my praise' as the direct object of 'keep silent' (following the LXX), whereas the Hebrew reads 'God of my praise, do not be silent.'
notes.108:6: Vulgate 'diabolus' ('the devil') renders Greek diabolos, corresponding to Hebrew satan ('an accuser' or 'adversary').
notes.108:8: Vulgate 'episcopatum' literally denotes an 'episcopate,' 'bishopric,' or 'office of oversight' (rendering Greek episkope), and is quoted of Judas in Acts 1:20.
notes.108:24: Vulgate 'propter oleum' ('because of oil,' following the LXX) literally renders the Hebrew expression usually understood as 'for lack of fat' or 'without oil.'
notes.108:31: Vulgate 'salvam faceret a persequentibus animam meam' follows the LXX in shifting from third-person 'the poor man' to first-person 'my soul' and reading 'persecutors' (against the Hebrew 'those who condemn his soul').
notes.109:3: Following the LXX, the Vulgate reads 'principium' ('sovereignty' or 'beginning'), 'in splendoribus sanctorum' ('in the splendors of the holy ones,' or 'of the saints'), and 'ex utero, ante luciferum, genui te' ('from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten You'), diverging sharply from the Hebrew MT.
notes.109:5: Vulgate 'confregit' uses the past/perfect tense ('has shattered,' following the LXX aorist), whereas the Hebrew is commonly rendered as future.
notes.109:6: Vulgate 'implebit ruinas' ('will fill up ruins,' from Greek ptomata, 'falls' or 'corpses') and plural 'capita in terra multorum' ('heads in the land of many') follow the LXX against the Hebrew ('fill with corpses; crush the head over a wide earth').
notes.110:2: Vulgate 'exquisita in omnes voluntates ejus' ('sought out for all His purposes,' literally 'wills,' following the LXX) differs from the Hebrew ('studied by all who delight in them').
notes.110:3: Vulgate 'Confessio' renders Greek exomologesis ('praise,' 'thanksgiving,' or 'confession'), corresponding to Hebrew hod ('splendor').
notes.110:6: The Clementine Vulgate uses the future tense 'annuntiabit' ('He will declare'), differing from both the Hebrew perfect and the LXX aorist ('He has declared').
notes.110:10: Vulgate masculine singular 'eum' ('it') refers grammatically to 'timor Domini' ('the fear of the Lord'), whereas the Hebrew has a plural pronoun referring to His precepts and the LXX has a feminine singular referring to wisdom.
notes.111:1: The Vulgate superscription "of the return of Haggai and Zechariah" follows the Septuagint and is absent from the Hebrew text (which numbers this Psalm 112). Latin "volet nimis" literally reads "will exceedingly wish/desire," rendering the biblical idiom for taking great delight.
notes.111:3: Vulgate "Gloria et divitiæ" ("Glory and wealth") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "wealth and riches."
notes.111:4: The Latin places the three adjectives ("merciful, and compassionate, and righteous") without a verb, leaving open whether they describe the Lord or the upright person.
notes.111:5: Vulgate "sermones suos" specifically means "his words" (following the Septuagint), whereas the underlying Hebrew term can mean either "words" or "affairs."
notes.111:10: Vulgate "Peccator" and "peccatorum" ("sinner"/"sinners") follow the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "wicked."
notes.112:1: Latin "pueri" (rendering Greek "paides") can mean either "servants" or "children"; unlike the Hebrew text (which numbers this Psalm 113), the Vulgate does not add "of the Lord" after "pueri."
notes.112:6: Vulgate "humilia respicit" ("looks upon lowly things") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "who humbles Himself to look."
notes.112:7: Vulgate "a terra" ("from the earth") follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew reads "from the dust," and "de stercore" literally means "from the dung."
notes.113:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate combines Hebrew Psalms 114 (vv. 1-8) and 115 (vv. 9-26) into a single psalm and places "Hallelujah" at its opening. Latin "populo barbaro" refers to a people of foreign speech.
notes.113:2: Vulgate "Judæa" ("Judea") follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew reads "Judah," and "sanctificatio" literally means "sanctification" or "sanctuary."
notes.113:7: Vulgate "mota est" ("was shaken") is a past passive indicative following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has an imperative ("tremble").
notes.113:17: Following the Septuagint, verses 17-19 use past indicative verbs ("hoped") rather than the Hebrew imperatives ("trust"), read "house of Israel" in verse 17, and render "protector" where the Hebrew has "shield"; verses 20-21 likewise use past tense ("blessed") where the Hebrew has future.
notes.113:25: Vulgate "in infernum" ("into the underworld," literally "the lower region/hell") renders Septuagint "Hades" where the Hebrew reads "into silence," and the Vulgate adds the vocative "Domine" ("Lord").
notes.114:1: Vulgate Psalm 114 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 116:1-9 (the Vulgate divides Hebrew Psalm 116 into Psalms 114 and 115). Latin Dilexi ("I have loved") has no explicit object, and exaudiet ("will listen to") is future tense, whereas many Hebrew-based translations read "I love the Lord, because He has heard."
notes.114:3: Latin pericula inferni ("the perils of the underworld") follows the Septuagint; infernus denotes the realm of the dead (also traditionally rendered "hell," corresponding to Hebrew Sheol), while pericula ("perils") differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "straits/distresses."
notes.114:6: Latin parvulos ("little ones"), following the Septuagint, corresponds to "the simple" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.114:8: Latin eripuit ("He has rescued") is third person, following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text addresses God in the second person ("You have rescued").
notes.114:9: Latin Placebo Domino ("I will be pleasing to the Lord"), following the Septuagint, corresponds to "I will walk before the Lord" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text; in regione vivorum is literally "in the region of the living."
notes.115:1: Vulgate Psalm 115 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 116:10-19. Latin Credidi, propter quod locutus sum ("I believed, for which reason I spoke," quoted via the Septuagint in 2 Corinthians 4:13) differs from Hebrew-based readings ("I believed even when I spoke"), and humiliatus sum ("I was brought low") repeats the exact verb used in 114:6.
notes.115:2: Latin in excessu meo (literally "in my going out [of myself]" or "in my ecstasy") translates Greek ekstasis to convey mental overwhelm or bewilderment, corresponding to "in my haste/alarm" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.115:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate repeats the verb retribuo in a relative clause (pro omnibus quae retribuit mihi, "for all that He has rendered to me"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text uses a noun phrase ("for all His benefits toward me").
notes.115:7: Latin quia ("for") literally reflects a particle in the vocative plea (often rendered "surely" or "indeed" from the Hebrew), and Dirupisti ("You have broken [apart]"), following the Septuagint, is stronger than Hebrew "You have loosed."
notes.115:8: Latin hostiam laudis ("a sacrifice of praise"), following the Septuagint, corresponds to "a sacrifice of thanksgiving" in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.116:1: Vulgate Psalm 116 corresponds to Hebrew Psalm 117, placing Alleluja ("Hallelujah") at the opening of this psalm rather than at the close of the previous one. Unlike the Hebrew and Septuagint, which use two distinct verbs ("praise" and "extol"), the Vulgate repeats the same verb (laudate) in both clauses.
notes.116:2: Latin confirmata est ("has been established/confirmed") reflects the Septuagint's passive verb where the Hebrew reads "is great/mighty," and veritas ("truth") corresponds to Hebrew emet (often rendered "faithfulness"). Unlike Hebrew Psalm 117:2, the Vulgate has no closing "Hallelujah" here.
notes.117:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate opens this psalm with Alleluja (Hallelujah), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text places it at the end of the preceding psalm. In v. 2, the Vulgate likewise includes quoniam bonus ("that He is good"), which is absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.117:10: Latin et in nomine Domini, quia ultus sum in eos retains the emphatic conjunction quia ("indeed") and uses the past tense "I took vengeance on them" (following the Septuagint; repeated in vv. 11-12), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads a future "I will cut them off."
notes.117:12: Latin exarserunt ("blazed up," following the Septuagint) contrasts with the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "they were extinguished."
notes.117:27: Latin Constituite diem solemnem in condensis, usque ad cornu altaris ("Establish a solemn day with dense boughs, up to the horn of the altar") follows the Septuagint in referring to a festival with thick foliage and uses the singular cornu ("horn"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text speaks of binding the festal sacrifice with cords up to the horns of the altar.
notes.117:28: The Clementine Vulgate repeats the closing sentence of v. 21 (Confitebor tibi quoniam exaudisti me, et factus es mihi in salutem), an addition absent from v. 28 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.118:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate opens Psalm 118 (Psalm 119 in Hebrew numbering) with "Hallelujah" (Latin Alleluja), which is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, and retains the Hebrew acrostic letter names heading each eight-verse stanza.
notes.118:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate makes the workers of iniquity the subject ("those who practice iniquity have not walked in His ways"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text continues describing the righteous ("they also do no iniquity; they walk in His ways").
notes.118:5: Latin justificationes (literally "justifications," calquing Greek dikaiomata) denotes God's righteous decrees or statutes and is rendered consistently as "ordinances" throughout this psalm.
notes.118:20: Latin concupivit ... desiderare ("has longed to desire," following the Septuagint) reflects a distinct reading from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which has "my soul is crushed with longing."
notes.118:28: Latin dormitavit ... prae taedio ("has grown drowsy from weariness," following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "my soul weeps [or melts away] from grief."
notes.118:51: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads inique agebant ("acted wickedly"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "utterly derided me."
notes.118:60: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads paratus sum, et non sum turbatus ("I am prepared, and I am not troubled"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "I hastened and did not delay."
notes.118:70: Following the Septuagint (which read Hebrew chalev, "milk," rather than chelev, "fat"), the Vulgate has coagulatum est sicut lac cor eorum ("their heart has curdled like milk"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "their heart is unfeeling like fat."
notes.118:83: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads in pruina ("in the frost"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "in the smoke."
notes.118:85: Following the Septuagint (which read Hebrew sichot, "tales," rather than shichot, "pits"), the Vulgate reads narraverunt mihi iniqui fabulationes ("the wicked have recounted fables to me"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "the arrogant have dug pits for me."
notes.118:91: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate makes "the day" (dies) the subject ("by Your ordering the day continues"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads adverbially ("by Your ordinances they stand to this day").
notes.118:112: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders Hebrew eqev as propter retributionem ("because of the reward"), whereas many translations from the Masoretic Text read "to the very end."
notes.118:119: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads praevaricantes reputavi omnes peccatores terrae ("I have counted all the sinners of the earth as transgressors"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "like dross You remove all the wicked of the earth."
notes.118:120: Following the Septuagint (which connected Hebrew samar with the root for "nail"), the Vulgate reads confige timore tuo carnes meas ("pierce through my flesh with the fear of You"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "my flesh trembles for fear of You."
notes.118:127: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders Hebrew paz ("refined gold") as topazion ("topaz").
notes.118:148: The Clementine Vulgate uniquely reads ad te diluculo ("to You at daybreak"), expanding on the Septuagint ("toward dawn"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "before the night watches."
notes.118:150: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads appropinquaverunt persequentes me iniquitati ("those who persecute me have drawn near to iniquity"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "those who pursue wicked schemes draw near."
notes.118:151: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads omnes viae tuae ("all Your ways"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "all Your commandments."
notes.118:160: Following the Septuagint (arche), the Vulgate renders Hebrew rosh as principium ("beginning"), whereas many translations from the Masoretic Text render it "sum" or "entirety."
notes.118:173: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads ut salvet me ("to save me"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "to help me."
notes.119:1: Latin "Canticum graduum" literally means "A song of steps" (corresponding to the traditional "Song of Ascents"). Latin "exaudivit" ("heard" favorably) follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "answered."
notes.119:3: Latin "ad linguam dolosam" ("for" or "against a deceitful tongue") uses a preposition with the accusative, following the Septuagint rather than the direct vocative ("you deceitful tongue") of the Hebrew. In verse 2, Latin "labiis iniquis" ("unjust lips") likewise follows the Septuagint against Hebrew "lying lips."
notes.119:4: Latin "carbonibus desolatoriis" ("desolating coals") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "coals of the broom tree."
notes.119:5: Latin "incolatus meus prolongatus est" ("my sojourn has been prolonged") follows the Septuagint where the Hebrew has the place name "Meshech." Vulgate "habitantibus Cedar" ("those who live in Kedar") also differs from Hebrew and Septuagint "tents of Kedar."
notes.119:7: Latin "impugnabant me gratis" ("they attacked me without cause") follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "they are for war." The Vulgate also places "with those who hate peace" at the start of verse 7 rather than the end of verse 6.
notes.120:1: The Clementine Vulgate uses the past tense "Levavi" ("I lifted," following the Septuagint against the Hebrew imperfect) and punctuates "unde veniet auxilium mihi." as a relative statement ("from where help will come to me") rather than a question.
notes.120:3: Latin "Non det in commotionem" literally means "May He not give into shaking/unsteadiness," using jussive subjunctives ("det," "dormitet") to express a blessing rather than the future indicative often translated from the Hebrew.
notes.120:5: Latin "protectio tua" ("your protection") follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew reads "your shade." The Vulgate also uses the present indicative "custodit" ("guards") here and in the first clause of verse 7.
notes.120:6: Latin "uret" ("will burn") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has "will strike."
notes.120:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate places "introitum" before "exitum" ("your coming in and your going out"), reversing the Hebrew order ("your going out and your coming in").
notes.121:1: Latin "in his quæ dicta sunt mihi" ("in the things that were spoken to me") uses a neuter plural passive construction, and "ibimus" ("We will go") is future indicative following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "when they said to me, 'Let us go.'"
notes.121:3: Latin literally reads "whose participation of it [is] in the very same" ("cujus participatio ejus in idipsum"), a calque of the Septuagint idiom meaning "together" or "in unity" with a Semitic resumptive pronoun; the Hebrew reads "that is bound firmly together." In verse 2, Latin "atriis" ("courts") also follows the Septuagint against Hebrew "gates."
notes.121:5: Latin literally reads "seats sat in judgment, seats over the house of David" ("sederunt sedes in judicio, sedes super domum David"), following the Septuagint "over the house" where the Hebrew reads "for judgment, the thrones of the house of David."
notes.121:6: Latin "abundantia" is nominative, forming a verbless blessing ("and [may there be] abundance for those who love you") that follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew verb "may they prosper."
notes.121:7: Following the Septuagint, Latin "in virtute tua" ("in your strength") and "in turribus tuis" ("in your towers") differ from the Hebrew "within your ramparts" and "within your palaces." In verses 8-9, the Vulgate also uses past tenses ("loquebar," "quæsivi") and "de te" ("concerning you") where the Hebrew has cohortatives and "within you."
notes.122:1: Latin Canticum graduum literally means "A song of steps," a heading shared by Psalms 119-133 (Hebrew 120-134) and traditionally associated with the Temple steps or pilgrimage ascents to Jerusalem.
notes.122:2: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses plural manibus ("hands") and dominorum ("masters"), with locative in manibus ("on the hands"), whereas the Hebrew has singular "hand" and "master."
notes.122:4: The Vulgate places opprobrium ("reproach") and despectio ("scorn") in the nominative with datives (abundantibus, superbis) rather than ablatives of filling as in v. 3, whereas the Hebrew reads "with the scoffing of those at ease, the contempt of the proud."
notes.123:1: The Vulgate reads in nobis (literally "in us" or "among us"), following the Septuagint, where the Hebrew means "on our side."
notes.123:3: Here and in vv. 4-5 the Vulgate reads forte/forsitan ("perhaps"), reflecting the Septuagint particle ara, whereas the Hebrew reads "then."
notes.123:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate makes "our soul" (anima nostra) the subject passing through "a torrent" (torrentem) and singular "unbearable water" (aquam intolerabilem), whereas the Hebrew makes the torrent and raging waters sweep over our soul.
notes.123:7: The Vulgate follows the Septuagint with passer ("sparrow"), venantium ("hunters"), and passive verbs (erepta est, liberati sumus), whereas the Hebrew has "bird," "fowlers," and "escaped."
notes.124:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate places qui habitat ("who dwells") at the end of v. 1 to join with in Jerusalem in v. 2, making the inhabitant of Jerusalem the subject of "will never be shaken" (literally "will not be shaken forever"); the Hebrew ends v. 1 with Mount Zion abiding forever.
notes.124:3: Unlike the Hebrew, where the scepter of wickedness is the subject and "will not rest," the Vulgate makes the Lord the explicit subject who "will not leave" (non relinquet) "the rod of sinners" (virgam peccatorum). The Latin punctuation here links the purpose clause ("so that...") to the petition in v. 4, though many editions end the sentence at v. 3.
notes.124:5: Latin in obligationes (literally "into bindings/obligations," here "into entanglements") renders the Septuagint word for "twistings" or "entanglements," whereas the Hebrew reads "to their crooked ways."
notes.125:1: Latin "Canticum graduum" ("A song of the steps," corresponding to Hebrew "ascents") is the traditional title of Psalms 119-133 in the Vulgate. Vulgate "sicut consolati" ("like those who have been comforted") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "like those who dream."
notes.125:2: Vulgate "dicent" is future tense ("they will say," following the Septuagint), where the Hebrew verb is normally rendered in the past ("they said"). "The Lord has done great things with them" renders the literal Hebraic Latin idiom "Magnificavit Dominus facere cum eis" ("the Lord has magnified to do with them").
notes.125:4: Vulgate "torrens in austro" ("a torrent in the south") is singular, following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has the plural "watercourses in the Negev."
notes.125:6: Vulgate uses plural verbs and a past-imperfect to future shift ("Euntes ibant et flebant... Venientes autem venient"), rendering the Hebrew emphatic infinitive absolutes via Septuagint plural participles; the Hebrew text is singular.
notes.126:1: The Vulgate shifts tense between the two halves of the verse, using the perfect "laboraverunt" ("have labored") in the first clause and the present "vigilat" ("stays awake") in the second.
notes.126:2: Vulgate "surgite postquam sederitis" ("rise after you have sat down") is an imperative following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "going late to rest." The final clause "Cum dederit dilectis suis somnum," ("When He gives sleep to His beloved,") introduces a temporal clause completed in v. 3, whereas the Hebrew reads "for so He gives to His beloved in sleep."
notes.126:4: Vulgate "filii excussorum" ("the sons of those who have been shaken out") follows the Septuagint, reflecting a different vocalization/root from the Hebrew Masoretic reading "sons of youth."
notes.126:5: Vulgate "desiderium suum" ("his desire") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "his quiver."
notes.127:1: Vulgate "Beati omnes qui timent... qui ambulant" is plural ("Blessed are all who fear... who walk"), following the Septuagint, where the Hebrew uses the singular ("everyone who fears...").
notes.127:2: Latin "Labores manuum tuarum quia manducabis" places "quia" ("because") after the fronted object and preserves the metonymy of eating one's "labors" (meaning the produce of one's work).
notes.127:3: Vulgate "vitis abundans in lateribus domus tuae" ("an abundant vine in the sides of your house") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "a fruitful vine within the innermost parts of your house."
notes.127:6: Vulgate "pacem" ("peace") is in the accusative case, making it grammatically a further direct object of "videas" ("may you see"), whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint treat it as an independent blessing ("Peace be upon Israel").
notes.128:1: Latin Canticum graduum ("A song of steps") renders the Septuagint title for the pilgrimage psalms (Psalms 119-133 in Vulgate numbering), traditionally associated with going up to Jerusalem or with the steps of the temple.
notes.128:3: Vulgate fabricaverunt peccatores; prolongaverunt iniquitatem suam ("sinners have built; they have prolonged their iniquity") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "plowmen plowed... they made long their furrows."
notes.128:4: Vulgate cervices peccatorum ("the necks of sinners") follows the Septuagint against the Hebrew Masoretic Text's "the cords of the wicked."
notes.129:3: Latin sustinere ("endure" here) is repeated twice in 129:5 in the sense of patiently "waiting" for the Lord and upon His word, reflecting the dual semantic range of Greek hypomeno.
notes.129:5: Vulgate propitiatio ("propitiation") and propter legem tuam ("because of Your law") follow the Septuagint tradition against the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("forgiveness, that You may be feared"). Note also the sudden shift from second person ("You") to third person ("His word").
notes.129:6: This Latin critical text merges the traditional verse 4 into 129:5 and omits the clause "From the morning watch until night, let Israel hope in the Lord" found in some Vulgate and Septuagint witnesses.
notes.130:2: Vulgate Si non humiliter sentiebam, sed exaltavi animam meam ("If I did not think humbly, but have exalted my soul") follows the Septuagint's conditional oath form against the Hebrew affirmation ("Surely I have calmed and quieted my soul"). Likewise, Vulgate retributio ("retribution") reflects reading the second Hebrew gamul ("weaned child") as gemul ("recompense").
notes.130:3: Latin ex hoc nunc et usque in saeculum, literally "from this now and even into the age," is the standard Vulgate idiom for "from now on and forever."
notes.131:1: Latin mansuetudinis ejus ("his gentleness") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "all his affliction/hardship." Canticum graduum ("A song of the steps") is the Vulgate title for the Psalms of Ascents (Psalms 119-133 in Vulgate numbering).
notes.131:5: The clause et requiem temporibus meis ("and rest to my temples," referring to the temples of the head) follows the Septuagint and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text. Verses 3-5 preserve the literal elliptical oath formula ("If I enter..."), implying "I surely will not."
notes.131:7: Latin in loco ubi steterunt pedes ejus ("at the place where His feet stood") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "at His footstool."
notes.131:15: Latin Viduam ejus ("her widow") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "her provisions."
notes.131:18: Latin sanctificatio mea ("My sanctification," matching sanctificationis tuae in v. 8 where Hebrew reads "Your strength") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "his crown."
notes.132:2: The Vulgate reads simply unguentum ("ointment") without the Hebrew adjective "precious," and renders oram vestimenti ejus ("the border of his garment") in the singular following the Septuagint rather than the Hebrew plural "his robes."
notes.132:3: The Vulgate reads singular montem Sion ("Mount Zion"), whereas the Hebrew and Septuagint have plural "mountains of Zion," and includes et ("and life forever") following the Septuagint.
notes.133:1: The closing phrase in atriis domus Dei nostri ("in the courts of the house of our God") follows the Septuagint and does not appear in the Hebrew Masoretic Text of this verse.
notes.133:2: The Vulgate opens v. 2 with In noctibus ("During the nights"), whereas the Hebrew places "by night" at the end of v. 1; in sancta is literally plural ("toward the holy places"), referring to the temple sanctuary.
notes.134:1: Latin "laudate, servi, Dominum" treats "servants" as a standalone vocative and "the Lord" as the direct object, following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "praise, servants of the Lord."
notes.134:5: Latin "Deus noster" ("our God") follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "our Lord."
notes.134:14: Latin "in servis suis deprecabitur" uses "deprecor" passively ("will be moved by prayer / pleaded with"), following the Septuagint ("will be consoled / appealed to"), whereas the Hebrew has "will have compassion on His servants."
notes.134:21: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate omits the closing "Hallelujah" found at the end of Hebrew Psalm 135:21, placing it instead at the opening of Vulgate Psalm 135:1.
notes.135:6: Latin "firmavit" ("established / made firm") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "spread out."
notes.135:10: Latin "cum primogenitis eorum" ("with their firstborn") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has "in their firstborn."
notes.135:12: Latin "brachio excelso" ("an uplifted arm") follows the Septuagint ("a high arm"), whereas the Hebrew has "an outstretched arm."
notes.135:23: Latin "Quia" ("Because") reflects the causal Septuagint reading, whereas the Hebrew is normally read as a relative clause ("who remembered us").
notes.135:26: The Clementine Vulgate includes a closing repetition of verse 3 ("Give thanks to the Lord of lords, for His mercy is forever") that is absent from the Hebrew text.
notes.136:1: Following the Septuagint tradition, the Vulgate includes the superscription "A psalm of David, of Jeremiah" (absent from the Hebrew text), associating this exilic lament with Jeremiah.
notes.136:2: Latin "organa" ("instruments") follows the Septuagint general term for musical instruments, whereas the Hebrew specifies "lyres" or "harps."
notes.136:3: Latin "qui abduxerunt nos" ("those who carried us away") and "Hymnum" ("a hymn") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "our tormentors [demanded] mirth."
notes.136:5: Latin "oblivioni detur" ("be given to oblivion") reflects the passive Septuagint reading ("be forgotten"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly understood actively ("let my right hand forget [its skill]").
notes.136:8: Latin "misera" ("wretched") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "devastated" or "doomed to destruction."
notes.137:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate includes "because You have heard the words of my mouth" (absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text) and reads "angels" (angelorum) where the Hebrew has elohim ("gods").
notes.137:2: Vulgate magnificasti super omne, nomen sanctum tuum ("magnified Your holy name above everything") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "magnified Your word above all Your name" (or "Your name and Your word above all").
notes.137:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate uses the imperative exaudi me ("hear me") and future multiplicabis ("You will multiply"), whereas the Hebrew uses past-tense verbs.
notes.137:8: Vulgate retribuet pro me ("will repay on my behalf") and ne despicias ("do not despise") reflect the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "will accomplish for me" and "do not forsake."
