notes.138:1: The superscription In finem ("To the end," also in 139:1) follows the Septuagint (eis to telos), corresponding to the Hebrew musical heading often rendered "For the choir director."
notes.138:3: Vulgate funiculum meum ("my cord" or "measuring line") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "my lying down."
notes.138:11: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads nox illuminatio mea in deliciis meis ("the night will be my illumination in my delights"), where the Hebrew has "the light around me will be night."
notes.138:16: Vulgate Imperfectum meum denotes an unformed or unfinished state; the closing clause Dies formabuntur, et nemo in eis ("Days will be formed, and no one will be in them") follows the Septuagint and the written Hebrew (Ketiv), whereas many translations follow the spoken Hebrew (Qere) "when as yet there was not one of them."
notes.138:17: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads amici tui ("Your friends") and principatus eorum ("their rule"), whereas the Hebrew reads "Your thoughts" and "their sum."
notes.138:20: Vulgate dicitis in cogitatione: Accipient in vanitate civitates tuas ("you say in thought, 'They will take Your cities in vain'") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew refers to enemies taking God's name in vain.
notes.139:9: Vulgate Ne tradas me, Domine, a desiderio meo peccatori ("Do not hand me over, Lord, from my desire to the sinner") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "Do not grant, Lord, the desires of the wicked."
notes.139:10: Vulgate Caput circuitus eorum ("The head of their encircling") follows the Septuagint, where the Hebrew has "the head of those who surround me."
notes.139:11: Vulgate in miseriis non subsistent ("in miseries they will not endure") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "into deep pits, that they may not rise."
notes.140:3: Latin 'ostium circumstantiae' ("a door of enclosure") follows the Septuagint ('perioches'), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "keep watch over the door of my lips."
notes.140:4: Latin 'verba malitiae' ("words of malice") and 'ad excusandas excusationes' ("to offer excuses") follow the Septuagint; 'electis eorum' can mean either "their chosen ones" or "their choice things" (the Hebrew reads "delicacies").
notes.140:5: Latin 'oleum peccatoris' ("a sinner's oil") and 'in beneplacitis eorum' ("in their good pleasures") follow the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "oil upon the head" and "against their evil deeds."
notes.140:6: Latin 'juncti petrae' ("joined to the rock") renders Greek 'echomena petras' ("close beside the rock"), and 'quoniam potuerunt' ("because they have prevailed") reflects a Greek variant meaning "were strong/able" rather than "were pleasant/sweet."
notes.140:10: Latin 'retiaculo ejus' ("his net") is grammatically ambiguous, referring either to the sinner's own net or to an adversary's.
notes.141:1: Latin 'Intellectus' ("Understanding") renders the Hebrew superscription 'maskil' via the Septuagint.
notes.141:4: Latin 'in deficiendo ... et' preserves the Septuagint and Hebraic construction connecting the failing of the psalmist's spirit with the preceding declaration or with God's knowledge of his paths.
notes.141:5: Latin 'Considerabam ... et videbam' ("I was looking closely ... and watching") uses first-person imperfect verbs following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew has imperatives ("Look ... and see").
notes.141:8: Latin 'me exspectant ... donec retribuas' ("are waiting for me until You reward me") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "will surround me, for You will deal bountifully with me."
notes.142:1: The historical notice "when his son Absalom was pursuing him" is present in the Vulgate and Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads only "A Psalm of David."
notes.142:2: Latin 'justificabitur' ("will be justified") follows the Septuagint future passive verb, whereas the Hebrew reads "is righteous."
notes.142:9: Latin 'ad te confugi' ("to You I have fled for refuge") follows the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew reads "to You I have hidden [myself]."
notes.142:10: Latin 'deducet' ("will lead") is future indicative (as are the verbs in verses 11-12), following the Septuagint rather than Hebrew jussives or imperatives; 'terram rectam' ("a level land") also carries the moral sense "upright."
notes.143:1: The superscription "Against Goliath" and the reading "my God" (where the Hebrew has "my rock") follow the Septuagint and are distinctive to the Vulgate tradition.
notes.143:3: Vulgate "innotuisti ei" ("You have become known to him," following the Septuagint) differs from the Hebrew Masoretic Text, which reads "that you know/regard him."
notes.143:12: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate renders vv. 12-14 in the third person ("whose sons... their daughters... their storehouses"), continuing the description of the "sons of foreigners" from v. 11, whereas the Hebrew reads first-person plural ("our sons").
notes.143:13: Vulgate "ex hoc in illud" ("from this into that," mirroring the Septuagint) reflects a different reading of the Hebrew expression usually rendered "of every kind" (literally "from kind to kind").
notes.143:15: Vulgate "Beatum dixerunt" ("They have called ... blessed," following the Septuagint) includes a verb absent from the Hebrew, contrasting popular praise of material prosperity (vv. 12-14) with true blessedness in the Lord.
notes.144:5: Here and in v. 6, the Vulgate (following the Septuagint) uses third-person plural verbs ("they will speak... recount") and reads "of Your holiness," where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has first-person singular verbs and "Your majesty."
notes.144:13: The second sentence ("Faithful is the Lord in all His words, and holy in all His works") preserves the "nun" stanza of this Hebrew alphabetical acrostic, attested in the Vulgate, Septuagint, Syriac, and Dead Sea Scrolls (11QPs-a) though absent from the Masoretic Text.
notes.144:14: Vulgate "elisos" ("those who are struck down," following the Septuagint; also in 145:8) contrasts with the Hebrew reading "those who are bowed down."
notes.144:16: Vulgate "benedictione" ("with blessing") reflects a distinctive reading compared with the Hebrew "with desire" and Septuagint "with good will/favor."
notes.145:1: The attribution to Haggai and Zechariah follows the Septuagint and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.145:4: Vulgate "cogitationes eorum" ("their thoughts," following the Septuagint) shifts to the plural pronoun referring back to princes and sons of men, whereas the Hebrew uses the singular ("his plans").
notes.145:8: Vulgate "illuminat caecos" ("gives light to the blind") differs in wording from both the Hebrew ("opens the eyes of the blind") and the Greek Septuagint ("makes the blind wise").
notes.145:9: Vulgate "vias peccatorum disperdet" ("will destroy the ways of sinners") has plural "ways" and "will destroy" (following the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew has singular "way of the wicked" and "makes crooked/brings to ruin."
notes.146:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate divides Hebrew Psalm 147 into two psalms: Psalm 146 (Hebrew 147:1-11) and Psalm 147 (Hebrew 147:12-20). Vulgate "for a psalm is good" (quoniam bonus est psalmus) uses the noun "psalm" rather than the Hebrew verbal phrase "to sing praises."
notes.146:3: Latin pairs the cognate terms contritos ("crushed") and contritiones (lit. "crushings" or "fractures," here "wounds").
notes.146:4: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "multitude" (multitudinem) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "number."
notes.146:8: The final clause "and vegetation for the service of mankind" (et herbam servituti hominum) follows the Septuagint (echoing Ps 103:14 Vulgate / 104:14 Hebrew) and is absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.147:1: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate treats Hebrew Psalm 147:12-20 as a separate psalm (Psalm 147) and opens it with "Hallelujah" (Alleluja), which is absent here in the Hebrew text.
notes.147:3: Latin fines tuos pacem uses a double accusative (lit. "your borders peace"), and adipe frumenti is literally "the fat of wheat," a biblical idiom for the richest, finest wheat.
notes.147:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "mist" (nebulam) where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "frost."
notes.147:7: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate casts all four verbs in the future tense and makes spiritus ("wind," which can also mean "breath" or "Spirit") the subject of the intransitive verb "will blow" (flabit), rather than the Hebrew causative "He makes His wind blow."
notes.147:9: Latin omni nationi is literally "for every nation," a biblical idiom with non meaning "for any nation." Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "He has not revealed His judgments to them" (judicia sua non manifestavit eis) with God as subject, whereas the Hebrew reads "they have not known them."
notes.148:2: Latin virtutes ("powers," rendering Septuagint dynameis for Hebrew "hosts") denotes the heavenly hosts or angelic powers.
notes.148:3: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads coordinate "all stars and light" (omnes stellae et lumen) rather than the Hebrew construct "all stars of light" (shining stars).
notes.148:5: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate includes "For He Himself spoke, and they came into being" (Quia ipse dixit, et facta sunt; cf. Ps 32:9 Vulgate / 33:9 Hebrew), a clause absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.148:8: Following the Septuagint, the Vulgate reads "ice" (glacies) where the Hebrew has "mist" or "smoke," and uses neuter plural quae faciunt ("which carry out"), referring to all the preceding elements rather than only the wind.
notes.148:14: Vulgate Confessio ejus (lit. "confession/thanksgiving of Him," following Septuagint exomologesis) corresponds to Hebrew "His majesty/splendor," and begins verse 14 here rather than concluding verse 13 as in the Hebrew numbering.
notes.149:1: Latin ecclesia sanctorum literally means "assembly of the saints" (or "holy ones"), where Vulgate sancti renders Greek hosioi (Hebrew chasidim, "godly/faithful ones").
notes.149:4: Vulgate exaltabit ... in salutem ("will exalt ... to salvation") follows the Septuagint verb ("exalt") with an accusative of goal ("to salvation"), whereas the Hebrew reads "adorns the afflicted with salvation."
notes.149:5: Vulgate Exsultabunt ... laetabuntur uses future indicative verbs ("will exult ... will be glad"), following the Septuagint, whereas the Hebrew uses jussives ("let them exult ...").
notes.149:7: Latin increpationes literally means "rebukes" or "reproofs" (following Septuagint elegmous), whereas the Hebrew counterpart is commonly rendered "punishments" or "chastisements."
notes.150:1: Vulgate Dominum ("the Lord") differs from both the Hebrew (El) and the Septuagint (theon, "God"). Latin in sanctis ejus is plural and can be parsed as neuter ("in His holy places," i.e., sanctuary) or masculine ("in His saints," a reading prominent in Latin patristic commentary).
notes.150:4: Latin choro (as in 149:3) denotes a choral dance (later also "choir"), and singular organo (from Greek organon) denotes an ancient wind instrument or pipe organ (corresponding to Hebrew ugav, a reed pipe or flute).
notes.150:5: Latin benesonantibus ("well-sounding," following Septuagint euechois) and jubilationis ("of jubilation") preserve the Vulgate-Septuagint wording rather than the Hebrew "sounding/clashing cymbals."
notes.150:6: Latin spiritus can mean either "spirit" or "breath" (translating Septuagint pnoe and Hebrew neshamah, "breath / living being"); Latin tradition widely takes Omnis spiritus as "every spirit."

unplaced.text: I will fulfill my vows to the Lord before all His people.
